items.title: A second Nakba? Palestinians in southern Syria fear Israeli expansion
items.author: Fadi Ibrahim, Francesca Maria Lorenzini
items.preview: Israel’s expanding military presence in southern Syria has revived fears of displacement among Palestinian families uprooted during the 1948 Nakba, raising the prospect of losing their homes for a second time. The post A second Nakba? Palestinians in southern Syria fear Israeli e
items.content: QUNEITRA — It was around 3 a.m. last year when a knock at the door woke Ahmad in his home. At first, he thought they were thieves. Then came a voice: “Don’t be afraid, this is the IDF. Calm down. Five hours and you’ll be back home.” Soldiers entered the house. A female officer accompanied by a dog followed, took his ID and phone from the table and inspected them. Outside, Ahmad estimated that more than 100 soldiers and 10 armored vehicles were waiting. His children were terrified. They took him outside and blindfolded him. Others stood beside him, their wrists were zip-tied. They took him to an elevated location in the occupied Golan Heights. “I couldn’t see anything,” he told Syria Direct , “but it was cold.” At around 5:30 a.m., an officer speaking broken Arabic began interrogating him about his family and daily activities. He also asked about Ahmad’s cousin, who remains in Israeli detention. “Tell the truth only and don’t lie,” Ahmad recalled the officer saying. “Keep eye contact and don’t look away. If you look away, you’re lying.” Then came a question: “Why are you observing us?” “I’m not. I wouldn’t want a confrontation with you.” Ahmad suspects the questioning was linked to information residents share in WhatsApp groups about Israeli military movements. He believes these groups have been infiltrated. “Where are you from?” one of them asked. “I’m from Beisan, Palestine,” Ahmad replied. The soldier seemed upset by Ahmad’s answer. He felt the soldier was about to strike him. But the soldier just looked at him and said: “You’re Syrian, not Palestinian.” Ahmad felt insulted. He was not in a position to contradict him. “As you wish,” he replied. The questioning lasted just five minutes, and he was released later that morning. This happened in Bassali, a small village in Quneitra governorate, southwestern Syria, last year. After the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Israeli troops crossed beyond the UN-monitored buffer zone and have regularly raided villages here and in western Daraa, searching homes and detaining residents. “Israel’s expanding military presence has raised fears of renewed displacement among Palestinian families who fled their homeland in 1948 and rebuilt their lives in southern Syria.” Israel’s expanding military presence has raised fears of renewed displacement among Palestinian families who fled their homeland in 1948 and rebuilt their lives in southern Syria. For families like Ahmad’s, the possibility of being uprooted again has revived memories of the Nakba , known to Arabs as “the catastrophe,” when their parents and grandparents were forced to flee Palestine as a result of the Arab-Israeli war of 1948. Under the 1974 Disengagement Agreement, signed after the 1973 war, no military forces other than UN peacekeepers could operate in a strip of land about 75 kilometers long separating the occupied Golan from the rest of Syria. The United Nations Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF) monitors it. Bassali lies outside that strip, on the Syrian side. Israel says the deal collapsed after Assad’s fall, prompting it to deploy troops into the buffer zone and establish a security zone beyond it. Initially described as temporary, the deployment has become open-ended, with Israeli officials citing jihadist threats and the protection of Syria’s Druze. The UN rejects that reading. In June 2026, the UN Security Council extended UNDOF’s mandate to December 31. A September report by the UN Secretary-General recorded continued violations and said Israeli forces held 11 positions on the Syrian side as of August 12, 2026. US-brokered talks on a security deal have not changed the situation on the ground. Damascus wants a deal based on the 1974 lines, while Israel links any withdrawal to a comprehensive peace agreement, according to Israeli public broadcaster Kan. The area is home to Palestinian families displaced in 1948 from what is now northern Israel, as well as their descendants, including Ahmad. A homeland preserved on paper This is particularly true for people like Abdul Karim Kheder, one of Ahmad’s relatives. Abdul Karim was born in 1946 in Kafr Misr, in the Beisan area of historic Palestine, now Israel. Two years later, his family fled during the Nakba. They took their livestock, spent a short time in Lebanon and eventually settled in Bassali. He was too young to remember the home they left behind. “My family used to tell me about Palestine, how the British came and a revolt broke out and failed,” he said, referring to the 1936–1939 Arab Revolt against British rule. He grew up hearing that, as the family prepared to leave, people in the village had said: “Whoever wants to surrender can surrender, and whoever wants to leave can leave!” His family chose to leave. His late father spoke of wanting to return, but never did. Ahmad, 41, was born in Bassali and grew up with that same expectation of return. “Our grandparents left, and we were deprived of our land,” he said. “We were fooled into thinking it would be a day or two and we would go back.” “Our grandparents left, and we were deprived of our land. We were fooled into thinking it would be a day or two and we would go back.” Beyond the stories passed down, there are papers to hold on to. Abdul Karim’s family, including his nephew Mohammad, keeps land-registration documents more than 80 years old in a binder. The paper has browned and the ink has faded, but the words “Government of Palestine” remain clear at the top. Some forms are printed in English, Arabic and Hebrew; one bears the British royal crest. Among them is a Barclays Bank slip dated 1941, carrying the name of Abdul Karim’s father, Ibrahim Kheder. “These documents are so precious we haven’t shown them to anyone,” a relative said as Mohammad opened the binder. General security checkpoint at the entrance of Quneitra. 25/10/2026 (Photo: Fadi Ibrahim) Although the family has kept the papers for land in Palestine they cannot reach, in Syria, they remain “temporary residents,” unable, they say, to own or register land in their own names. Under Syria’s longstanding policy toward Palestinian refugees, granting citizenship was seen as undermining the Palestinian right of return. It would give tacit legitimacy to the “Zionist entity,” as Israel is referred to in Syria and the broader Arab world. A 1956 law gave those registered with its refugee authority the same rights as Syrians in work, trade and military service, while letting them keep their Palestinian nationality. Property was the exception. Palestinians can own a house, but not agricultural, industrial or commercial real estate, according to the European Union Agency for Asylum. Read more: In southern Syria, echoes of the US-Israeli war with Iran hit close to home Mohammad and other villagers in Bassali work on other people’s farmland as laborers. They are neither tenants nor sharecroppers. For them, the law sets a ceiling: they can earn a wage from the land, but never own it. Ahmad feels a strong attachment to his Palestinian identity, yet he sees Syrians and Palestinians as sharing the same reality. “There is no difference between us,” he said. For a younger generation born and raised in Syria, that sense of belonging exists alongside ties to a Palestine they have never seen. Hamzeh, 30, was born in Daraa’s Palestinian refugee camp to a family originally from Tiberias, in present-day Israel. He runs a small shop, has a gentle smile and chooses his words carefully. In the camp, he said, nationality rarely entered everyday conversations. “When we talk to Syrians, we don’t ask them what their nationality is.” The authorities, however, treated them differently, he recalled. Under Assad, traveling from Daraa to university in Damascus meant passing through checkpoints where being Palestinian could bring additional scrutiny. “There was harshness toward some Palestinians in the regime’s days,” he said. In 2016, Hamzeh left for Germany through Turkey and Greece, adapting quickly to life there. Yet his registration as a stateless person, not as a Syrian citizen, remained a reminder of his unresolved status. After the fall of Assad, he withdrew his citizenship application and returned to Daraa to see the people and places he had left behind. Abandoned T52 tank from the former regime in Quneitra. 25/10/2026 (Photo: Fadi Ibrahim) The camp he returned to was heavily damaged, with roofless buildings riddled with bullet holes. But the soul of Palestine remains alive: residents still organize events celebrating Palestinian heritage, bringing out traditional clothing, food and carpets. Some families preserve belongings passed down from their grandparents, while others even keep the keys to their homes in Palestine. Asked about Israel’s expanding military presence in Syria, Hamzeh said that in the camp, residents often joke about it and do not take the threat too seriously. But in Bassali, the fear is harder to laugh off. “People fear they [the Israelis] will reach us,” Ahmad said. Since November 2022, Israeli forces have been building a road and an earthen berm known as Sufa 53 through southern Quneitra. Syria’s Foreign Ministry called the work a “flagrant breach” of the 1974 agreement. But Ahmad still believes that his family’s future remains tied to Palestine. “We are certain this land will be liberated and we will return to it, perhaps not us as individuals but the generations after us, our children or our grandchildren.” “We are certain this land will be liberated and we will return to it, perhaps not us as individuals but the generations after us, our children or our grandchildren.” For Abdul Karim, the prospect of being forced to leave raises a question he has faced before. Palestinians once kept out of Syrian politics, he said, only to be told, when trouble came, “to go somewhere else.” But where will they go? Note: Ahmad and Hamzeh are pseudonyms, as our sources did not want to use their real names. The post A second Nakba? Palestinians in southern Syria fear Israeli expansion appeared first on Syria Direct .

items.title: Italy backs rapid German membership path into GCAP fighter program
items.author: Tom Kington
items.preview: Italy has strongly denied a press report suggesting it opposes granting Germany partner status on the GCAP fighter program, claiming instead it fully backs German membership.
items.content: ROME — Italy has strongly denied a press report suggesting it opposes granting Germany partner status on the GCAP fighter program, claiming instead it fully backs German membership. The unusually long rebuttal from the Italian ministry of defense followed a report in the Financial Times on Saturday that defense minister Guido Crosetto used a video conference call last week with other representatives of the Italian-UK-Japan fighter to oppose making Germany a member. Berlin is mulling signing up to the program after the collapse of its talks with France to develop a rival sixth-generation jet. The press report suggested Italy was pushing to hand Germany observer status on the program rather than full membership, although it did quote an Italian official saying German membership could follow. Within hours of the report appearing, Crosetto’s ministry fired off a statement calling the article “entirely misleading”, adding it “does not reflect the position Italy has consistently maintained.” The statement agreed that it wanted Germany to obtain observer status, but in order to accelerate full membership status, not to delay or block it. “Italy has always expressed its full willingness to welcome Germany into the program. Indeed, precisely to facilitate and accelerate this process, Italy proposed that Germany joins as an observer, as an immediate, Program information-sharing enabler towards subsequent full membership,” it added. The statement added, “This proposal was not intended to limit Germany’s future role in the program. Quite the opposite: it was designed to speed up the conditions for its involvement as quickly as possible, while safeguarding the program’s progress and established timetable.” The talks come as the GCAP program picks up speed after the three nation partners handed a £4.6 billion ($6.1 billion) development contract to their national champions building the jet in July. Rome has spent €875 million ($970 million) this year on development . Canada has meanwhile already taken observer status on the program. The Italian statement said, “It is therefore totally false any reporting on opposition to Germany’s participation. Italy has demonstrated, through its actions and proposals, that it considers Germany’s involvement a positive opportunity.” It added, “Our priority remains ensuring that GCAP proceeds according to its agreed schedule, while creating the conditions for new partners to join through a clear and effective process. Italy is supporting, without delay, all the conditions to welcome Germany’s participation in the GCAP as soon as possible.”

items.title: Turkey says Hezbollah won’t disarm while Israel occupies Lebanese territory
items.author: Ragip Soylu
items.preview: Turkey says Hezbollah won’t disarm while Israel occupies Lebanese territory Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Mon, 11/16/2026 - 13:01 Ankara urges Washington to curb Israel’s actions and warns that Syrian intervention to disarm Hezbollah could trigger another civil war in Lebanon Suppo
items.content: Turkey says Hezbollah won’t disarm while Israel occupies Lebanese territory Submitted by Ragip Soylu on Mon, 11/16/2026 - 13:01 Ankara urges Washington to curb Israel’s actions and warns that Syrian intervention to disarm Hezbollah could trigger another civil war in Lebanon Supporters of Lebanese Shia movement Hezbollah wave flags of the group as they attend a ceremony commemorating Martyrs' Day in Beirut's southern suburbs on 11 November 2026 (Joseph Eid/AFP) Off Hezbollah’s disarmament in Lebanon can ultimately be achieved only if Israel ends its occupation of Lebanese territory, a Turkish official told Middle East Eye. Ankara has stepped up its engagement with the Lebanese government in recent months, including a visit to Turkey by Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in July. Bilal Erdogan, the Turkish president’s son, also made a three-day trip to Lebanon last week, meeting officials, dignitaries and community leaders. Several Ankara insiders told Middle East Eye that Turkey was seeking to deepen its ties across the Levant, particularly following the rise of a new Syrian government in Damascus. That transition has allowed Turkish officials to encourage dialogue between Syria and Lebanon. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani visited Beirut in July, in a trip described as opening a new chapter in relations between the two countries. Ankara believes stability in Syria can be achieved only if Lebanon is also stable. “I think we consider the relationship between Iraq , Syria and Lebanon as one big belt of strategic significance for security and safety in the whole region,” a Turkish official told MEE, speaking on condition of anonymity. He said Turkey would encourage cooperation between the three countries to ease regional tensions. Sohaib Jawhar, a Lebanese researcher, told MEE that Ankara increasingly views Lebanon as part of Syria’s strategic environment. It recognises that stability in Lebanon, particularly in the north, is essential to Syria’s stability, successful reconstruction and regional economic integration. Jawhar said Turkey was concerned that recent arrangements between Israel, Cyprus and Greece in the Eastern Mediterranean could consolidate a regional order that excludes Ankara. He added that Bilal Erdogan’s visit to Beirut was an attempt to broaden Turkey’s relations within Lebanon beyond its traditional Sunni Arab contacts to include a wider range of political and religious communities. During the trip, Erdogan’s son met representatives of the country’s Christian, Druze and Alawite communities. Footage of the rousing welcome he received in the Sunni stronghold of Tripoli circulated widely on social media, reviving rumours that Ankara plans to unite Lebanon’s Sunni political forces. A source familiar with the visit told MEE that Bilal Erdogan had discussed nothing of the sort, adding that the trip was intended to build closer ties between the two countries. Hezbollah’s arms Hezbollah’s future remains a central question for Lebanon. Although repeated assassinations and attacks targeting its leaders and rank-and-file members have weakened the movement, it has found ways to regroup and continue confronting Israel. The Turkish official accused Israel of creating facts on the ground rather than honouring its commitments. He said that although Hezbollah had withdrawn north of the Litani River, Israel had failed to keep its promise not to establish additional military outposts on Lebanese territory. 'So you ask Hezbollah to disarm at the moment when Israeli occupation continues to grow' - Turkish official “So you ask Hezbollah to disarm at the moment when Israeli occupation continues to grow,” the official said. “That’s an impossible equation that has to stop.” Israel invaded Lebanon in March, after Hezbollah renewed its rocket attacks on Israel in response to the war that the US and Israel launched against Iran on 28 February. Subsequent US-brokered talks between Israel and the Lebanese government secured a framework envisaging a gradual Israeli withdrawal as Lebanese authorities disarm Hezbollah and deploy across the country’s south. The arrangement has already been implemented in certain “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon, but progress has stalled in recent months. The official said Turkey had told US counterparts that their plan for Lebanon could succeed only if they halted Israel’s actions. Otherwise, he said, Hezbollah would not disarm. US President Donald Trump has floated the idea that Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa could intervene in Lebanon to secure Hezbollah’s disarmament. Damascus has publicly rejected that option. Ankara also believes it would fail and could trigger another civil war in Lebanon. Can Hezbollah salvage Syrian networks without clashing with Damascus? Read More » “Asking Syria to deal with the so-called Hezbollah issue or Lebanese issue without addressing the Israeli component is just impossible to do as long as Israel continues its occupation of southern Lebanon,” the official said. He accused Israel of entrenching its presence by establishing more temporary military posts and converting some into permanent positions. Jawhar said Ankara recognises that Hezbollah’s disarmament cannot be addressed independently of the political and security environment that gave rise to the group. “Israel’s continued occupation of Lebanese territory and its ongoing attacks provide Hezbollah with a fundamental justification for retaining its weapons, alongside the group’s more recent arguments concerning what it perceives as an existential threat emanating from Syria,” he said. “Turkey’s position does not necessarily imply support for Hezbollah’s continued existence as an armed force operating independently of the state, as demonstrated by Ankara’s role in efforts to bring weapons under state control in Iraq.” Israel-Syria negotiations Israel and Syria held negotiations earlier this year on a security agreement based on their 1974 disengagement accord. The Turkish official said Ankara had spent a year trying to bring Israeli and Syrian officials to the negotiating table to reach an understanding on southern Syria. He added that Turkey had proposed updating the existing agreement. Why is Syria considering joining the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact? Read More » “As expected, the Israelis refused,” the official said. “They don’t want to sign anything and they don’t want to stop anyways.” Turkish officials believe this reluctance explains why Israel puts forward proposals it knows Lebanon and Syria will reject. A senior Israeli official, however, blamed Syria for the lack of progress, telling the media in September that Damascus had lost its appetite for a deal after international sanctions were lifted. The Israeli official said Israel was unwilling to accept an agreement that would require it to withdraw from the buffer zone it created after the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, describing the zone as a security asset. Ankara nevertheless believes a new Israeli government could take a more pragmatic approach, potentially allowing rapid progress in Lebanon. “But again, as long as expansionism continues into Syria, into Lebanon, of course, what they’re doing in Gaza and the West Bank, these coffins will continue to roll and create more problems for the region,” the Turkish official said. Jawhar said Turkey could help develop an approach linking a complete Israeli withdrawal and an end to Israeli attacks with a stronger Lebanese Armed Forces and an internal dialogue aimed at gradually establishing the state’s monopoly over arms. “Turkey’s relations with Iran, its channels of communication with Lebanese political forces, and its relationship with the US administration also position Ankara to contribute to a political and security settlement, although its ability to directly influence Hezbollah’s decision-making remains limited,” he said. items.content: تُشير التقارير إلى أن شركة أبل تُحضّر لأربعة تحسينات رئيسية لهاتفها القابل للطي من الجيل الثاني، بما في ذلك ميزة التعرف على الوجه (Face ID)، وزر الإجراءات (Action Button)، وقدرات كاميرا مُحسّنة. مع ذلك، قد لا تُطرح إحدى أكثر الميزات ترقباً في موعد الإطلاق المُحدد لعام 2027، بل ستُطرح في طراز لاحق. ووفقاً لمارك غورمان من بلومبيرغ، تُولي أبل أولوية قصوى لتقنية التعرف على الوجه (Face ID) في هاتف iPhone Duo 2، المُقرر إطلاقه في خريف 2027. وقد طوّرت الشركة بالفعل نماذج أولية مزودة بتقنية التعرف على الوجه، لكن المهندسين ما زالوا يعملون على دمجها في الشاشة الخارجية. في ما يأتي 4 تغييرات تُشير التقارير إلى أن أبل تُفكّر في إضافتها إلى هاتفها القابل للطي القادم: iPhone Duo 2: تحسينات رئيسية مُتوقعة - Face ID: تعمل أبل على دمج تقنية التعرف على الوجه في الشاشة الخارجية، ما يسمح للمستخدمين بفتح الهاتف دون الحاجة إلى فتحه. - زر الإجراءات (Action Button): تستكشف الشركة وظائف جديدة تُمكّن المستخدمين من تخصيص وظيفة الضغط المطوّل على زر التحكم بالكاميرا لتشغيل تطبيقاتهم المُفضّلة. - كاميرا التقريب: من بين التحسينات التي تُفكّر أبل في إضافتها إلى كاميرا الجيل القادم من الهواتف القابلة للطي، عدسة تقريب مُخصصة. - تصميم أنحف وأخف وزناً: تسعى آبل أيضاً إلى تقليل سمك الجهاز ووزنه، ما يُحسّن من سهولة حمله. قد يتأخر إطلاق ميزة Face ID يستخدم الطراز الحالي، المُقرر إطلاقه في أكتوبر/تشرين الأول 2026، مستشعر بصمة مدمجاً في زر التشغيل الجانبي. أما الجيل الثاني من الجهاز فمن المتوقع أن يتضمن ميزة التعرّف على الوجه على شاشته الخارجية، ما يسمح للمستخدمين بفتحه دون الحاجة إلى فتحه. وصرح غورمان أنه لا يزال من غير المؤكد ما إذا كانت ميزة Face ID ستُدرج في النسخة النهائية. إذا لم يتمكن المهندسون من إنجاز العمل في الوقت المحدد، فقد تُضاف الميزة إلى iPhone Duo 3، ومن المحتمل أن تصل في عام 2028.

items.title: Bandits abduct 12 in Kaduna community, 14 now held captive
items.author: Nwafor
items.preview: By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo Suspected bandits have abducted 12 residents of Kurmin Wali community in Afogo Ward, Kajuru Local Government Area of Kaduna State, in a fresh attack that has left 14 people in captivity. The attack reportedly occurred on Sunday, November 15, 2026, when arme
items.content: By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo Suspected bandits have abducted 12 residents of Kurmin Wali community in Afogo Ward, Kajuru Local Government Area of Kaduna State, in a fresh attack that has left 14 people in captivity. The attack reportedly occurred on Sunday, November 15, 2026, when armed men invaded the community at about 9:14am and abducted 12 residents. The village head, Isiaku Danazumi, who confirmed the incident on Monday, said three of the abducted residents had escaped and returned to the community, while nine others remained in the custody of their abductors. He explained that the nine victims, alongside five other residents abducted in two separate attacks in October, brought the total number of people still being held by the bandits to 14. “Yes, the incident happened on Sunday around 9:14am. Twelve people were abducted by the bandits, but three returned, while the remaining nine are still with them. “But on October 2, 2026, two people were also abducted during the rainy season. Again, on October 10, three other people were abducted. So, in total, 14 of our people are with the bandits in the bush,” he said. The traditional ruler expressed concern over the recurring abductions, saying that although the relevant authorities had been notified, no concrete action had been taken to secure the victims’ release. He further disclosed that some security personnel visited the community on Sunday after the attackers had fled but reportedly left less than an hour after arriving. The latest attack has heightened concerns over the security situation in Kurmin Wali, which attracted national attention in January 2026 when suspected bandits abducted more than 80 residents during a church service. The mass abduction sparked widespread outrage and renewed calls for urgent government intervention to protect vulnerable communities in Kaduna State. As of the time of filing this report, the Kaduna State Police Command and the Ministry of Internal Security and Home Affairs had yet to issue official statements on Sunday’s attack. items.title: Oyo proposes N1.115trn 2027 budget, targets jobs, infrastructure
items.author: Nwafor
items.preview: By Adeola Badru The Oyo State Government has proposed a N1.115 trillion budget for 2027, prioritising infrastructure development, job creation, entrepreneurship and the growth of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) to accelerate economic expansion and improve residents’ l
items.content: By Adeola Badru The Oyo State Government has proposed a N1.115 trillion budget for 2027, prioritising infrastructure development, job creation, entrepreneurship and the growth of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) to accelerate economic expansion and improve residents’ living standards. The proposed budget, tagged “Budget of Sustained Progress,” is designed to consolidate gains recorded across critical sectors while strengthening the state’s economic competitiveness through investments in infrastructure, agriculture, human capital development and public-private partnerships. Governor Seyi Makinde presented the proposal to the Oyo State House of Assembly last week, with capital expenditure accounting for 60.1 per cent of the total spending plan. Speaking during the presentation of the budget breakdown and analysis at the Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning in Ibadan on Monday, the Permanent Secretary, Julius Ayanleke, said the proposal aligned with the administration’s vision of making Oyo State the fastest-growing economy in Nigeria. He said the government’s spending priorities would focus on completing ongoing projects, strengthening Internally Generated Revenue (IGR), attracting public and private investments, supporting MSMEs, expanding infrastructure and ensuring efficient utilisation of resources through Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs). According to Ayanleke, the proposed budget comprises N670.03 billion for capital expenditure, representing 60.1 per cent, and N445.31 billion for recurrent expenditure, accounting for the remaining 39.9 per cent. He explained that the substantial allocation to capital projects was intended to sustain the state’s development drive, particularly through the completion of ongoing projects and execution of critical infrastructure programmes. Among the projects earmarked for priority funding are the Ibadan Circular Road, Ido-Eruwa Road and several rural road projects, which he said had received adequate provisions to facilitate their timely completion. Providing an update on the state’s fiscal performance, Ayanleke disclosed that Oyo generated N618.72 billion between January and September 2026. He said the revenue comprised N401.44 billion in recurrent revenue and N217.28 billion in capital receipts. The permanent secretary explained that the 2027 budget was developed through the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF), sectoral planning processes and consultations with stakeholders across the state’s seven geopolitical zones to ensure that the spending priorities reflected residents’ development needs. Outlining the government’s fiscal targets, he said the administration would prioritise the completion of ongoing projects, reduce non-essential overhead costs and improve efficiency in personnel and recurrent expenditure. He added that the government was targeting a minimum annual growth of 10 per cent in IGR between 2027 and 2029, while ensuring that recurrent expenditure was financed through sustainable revenue sources. Other priorities, according to him, include diversifying the state’s revenue base, accelerating critical capital projects and expanding access to grants, development funding and public-private partnership arrangements. Ayanleke said maintaining the 60:40 capital-to-recurrent expenditure ratio demonstrated the government’s commitment to development-focused investments and long-term economic growth. He added that the spending approach would enable the state to channel more resources into productive investments capable of stimulating economic activities, supporting businesses, creating employment opportunities and improving residents’ welfare. Also speaking, the Executive Assistant to the Governor on Finance, Budget and Economic Planning, Gafar Bello, commended the state’s budget performance since 2019, attributing the progress to transparency, fiscal discipline, efficiency and effective deployment of fiscal management tools. Bello said the administration’s approach to fiscal management had contributed to improved budget implementation and strengthened the state’s capacity to pursue its development objectives. In his remarks, the President of the Multi-disciplinary Finance Professionals (MFP), Dr Oyedepo Oyebade, praised the state government and the Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning for what he described as the transparent presentation of the 2027 budget and impressive implementation of the 2026 fiscal proposal. Oyebade particularly highlighted the state’s 103 per cent performance on statutory allocation on a pro-rata basis, saying it reflected the adoption of prudent and realistic revenue projections. He also commended the government for sustaining transparency, accountability and the January-to-December budget cycle, describing the consistency as an important feature of sound fiscal management. According to him, allocating about 60 per cent of the proposed budget to capital projects underscored the administration’s commitment to completing ongoing projects, expanding infrastructure and driving development across the state. items.title: 2027: Tinubu’ll get over 80% votes in Ebonyi, Nwifuru vows
items.author: Nwafor
items.preview: By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki Governor Francis Nwifuru of Ebonyi State has vowed to deliver more than 80 per cent of the state’s votes to President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 general election, citing what he described as the President’s contributions to the state and its people. Nwifuru
items.content: By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki Governor Francis Nwifuru of Ebonyi State has vowed to deliver more than 80 per cent of the state’s votes to President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 general election, citing what he described as the President’s contributions to the state and its people. Nwifuru said Tinubu had demonstrated commitment to Ebonyi through key appointments, particularly the appointment of former Governor David Umahi as Minister of Works. The governor spoke during the inauguration of the President Bola Ahmed Tinubu (PBAT) Door-to-Door Campaign Movement at Unity Square, Abakaliki, where he also commended the group’s initiator, Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo, for mobilising support for the President’s re-election. He described Umahi’s appointment as a significant recognition of the South-East, noting that the region had not previously occupied the position of Minister of Works. “Most importantly, like we said during the presidential campaign inauguration here, he has appointed our son, our brother, our ally, our father, the Minister of Works of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. And he is a true supporter of our dear President. “I am feeling very, very grateful to our dear brother, Tompolo, for this show of love and show of gratitude,” he said. Nwifuru described Tinubu as an exceptional leader who had supported youths and other Nigerians, adding that his administration’s actions had strengthened the state’s commitment to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC). He said the President’s appointments and other interventions had convinced the people of Ebonyi to support his re-election bid. “We do not want anybody to embarrass us because what the President has done to us has convinced us. And we are ready to vote for him beyond 80 per cent. “Our people are well educated. They are well enlightened. They are aware of the sacrifices Mr President has made,” the governor said. He also urged residents to vote massively for APC candidates in the 2027 elections, describing the party’s performance in the state as deserving of electoral support. “And the party has done tremendously well for our people here. We are indebted to the party. And to pay the party back is to vote for APC party massively from top to bottom,” he added. Speaking at the event, the National Coordinator of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, Government Tompolo, who was represented by the Managing Director of Tantita Security Services, Kestin Pondi, said the movement was established to take the President’s re-election campaign directly to households across the country. Pondi described Tinubu as a courageous leader who had embarked on economic reforms from the beginning of his administration and sustained them despite the challenges. He said the movement’s slogan, “Every Door Matters”, reflected its commitment to reaching Nigerians at the grassroots and mobilising support for the President. According to him, Tinubu’s policies, including the removal of petrol subsidy, had helped state governments meet their salary obligations and address economic challenges. He also claimed that the naira was strengthening, the economy was stabilising and fuel queues had eased under the administration. “Today, we are not having fuel queues, though we are almost in December, because President Tinubu knows what he is doing. And we need to give him another four years for him to consolidate on what he has started,” Pondi said. He disclosed that the movement had visited 26 states, including the Federal Capital Territory, as part of its nationwide mobilisation campaign. items.title: Britain and France failed this war – and lost their imperial grip
items.author: RT
items.preview: The 1956 invasion of Egypt exposed the limits of European power and hastened the collapse of colonial rule across Africa and the Middle East Read Full Article at RT.com
items.content: The 1956 invasion of Egypt exposed the limits of European power and hastened the collapse of colonial rule across Africa and the Middle East Seventy years ago, the global balance of power shifted forever during the 1956 Suez Crisis. What began as a secret tripartite pact between Britain, France, and Israel erupted into a military invasion of Egypt in late October. Although allied forces first seized parts of the Sinai and Port Said, they were forced into a humiliating retreat that marked the twilight of European colonial dominance. Just four years since the July 1952 revolution that overthrew Egypt’s pro-Western monarchy, both France and Britain began to realize that Gamal Abdel Nasser, a new figure in Cairo, was not just a temporary military strongman. By early 1956, Paris recognized him as an existential threat to Algérie française – its long-term project to treat Algeria not as a colony, but as an integral overseas department (département d’outre-mer) and an unyielding extension of metropolitan France. Read more Former colony demands truth, France prefers amnesia Cairo had rapidly become the political and logistical heartland of the Algerian independence movement, providing sanctuary, funding, and powerful propaganda broadcasts via Voice of the Arabs to Algeria’s National Liberation Front (FLN), whose independence uprising began in 1954. London saw the shift in Egypt as a direct threat to the remnants of its African empire, one that risked triggering a wider unravelling across its regional spheres. The dismantling of the old pro-Western order meant the architecture of the Middle East was changing forever. This was the historical pivot that had for centuries enabled the British Empire’s connections to its vital imperial arteries, stretching from Aden and the Persian Gulf to the Indian Ocean and beyond. As the British Empire faded, it had become far more critical as the shortest connection to Persian Gulf oil. By mid-1956, that anxiety curdled into desperation. British Prime Minister Anthony Eden and his chancellor of the exchequer, Harold Macmillan, who later became prime minister and was even more uncompromisingly hawkish on Nasser, viewed the Egyptian leader through a crude, reductionist lens, branding him an “Asiatic Mussolini” and a dictator who had to be permanently neutralized before British influence collapsed entirely. Meanwhile, in Paris, Guy Mollet’s government was convinced that severing the head of Arab republicanism that Nasser was preaching out of Cairo was the only way to crush the Algerian rebellion at its source. This convergence of imperial panic birthed the Sèvres Protocol – a secret tripartite conspiracy uniting Britain, France, and Israel. The plan was simple: Israel would strike across the Sinai desert, providing London and Paris with the pretext to “intervene” as neutral peacekeepers, seize back the Suez Canal, and topple Nasser in one swift blow. Just four years after the 1952 revolution, on July 26, Nasser had nationalized the waterway, which was not only a vital source of income for Egypt, but a pillar of national sovereignty and security. Instead of breaking him, the allied aggressors walked straight into a geopolitical trap that exposed the hollowed-out foundations of European power and altered the map of the region. Read more The high dam diplomacy: When the USSR tamed the Nile The tripartite plan materialized as a full-scale military invasion of Egypt in October and November 1956, involving British, French, and Israeli forces. While the allied armies managed to capture parts of the Sinai and Port Said, on the western shores of the canal, on the ground, the aggression collapsed under intense diplomatic and economic pressure from Washington and Moscow, forcing a humiliating withdrawal already by late 1956. Egypt’s resistance against the Tripartite Aggression transformed into a rallying cry for Nasser across the Arab world, where he was already immensely popular. Far from breaking him, let alone toppling him, or reclaiming lost imperial prestige, the fiasco shattered the myth of Western invincibility, and cemented Cairo as the beating heart of anti-colonial resistance across the Middle East and Africa. By invading Egypt, Britain and France sought to keep control of the canal, which the joint British-French company had operated since its opening in 1869, denying Egypt its national rights over its own sovereign territory, the economic benefits it generated, and the full exercise of its independence. For Israel, it was about breaking a strategic waterway controlled by a sworn foe and projecting military force into the future of the already ongoing conflict with Egypt, as well as the wider Arab cause tied to Palestine since Israel’s creation. But as entire enterprise ended in failure, it signaled the end of British dominance in the region, and further damaged its standing across Africa. There, former colonies were gaining independence, fueled in no small part by Nasser and his support for almost all African liberation movements, from Algeria to sub-Saharan struggles stretching from Kenya to Ghana. The political fallout across the waning British Empire and the broader developing world was unforgiving. At the London meetings and through Commonwealth diplomatic channels, the invasion triggered hostility from emerging member states like India, whose Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru condemned the aggression as a dangerous throwback to 19th-century imperialism. Read more Meet the colonel who defied Britain, challenged Israel, and became a godlike hero to Gaddafi and millions of Arabs Across Africa, the shockwaves were felt immediately. For the Gold Coast, where Britain had already conceded independence in principle after Kwame Nkrumah’s party won the July 1956 elections , the case of Suez was indicative. An empire that could not force its will on Egypt was in no position to hold back Africans demanding self-rule. Ghana became independent in March 1957. Though the Non-Aligned Movement would not be formally institutionalized until 1961, the crisis served as the ultimate trial by fire for the “Bandung Spirit” born a year earlier. From Sudan to newly independent Morocco and Tunisia, public and political opinion rallied behind Cairo, proving that a sovereign post-colonial state could defy Western gunboat diplomacy and rewrite the geopolitical order. The Egyptian debacle also shattered what remained of Anglo-French strategic unity in Africa. By exposing that neither London nor Paris could mount a major military operation without American acquiescence, Suez accelerated the liquidation of empire. In France, the attempt to save Algérie française by striking Egypt backfired: It did not cut the FLN’s lifeline, it strained the French treasury, and helped bring down the Fourth Republic by 1958. For Britain, Suez was a turning point. Within three months of becoming prime minister in January 1957, Macmillan met US President Dwight D. Eisenhower in Bermuda to rebuild the Anglo-American alliance, with colonial policy on the agenda. Scholars see his government’s attempt to set a new foreign policy agenda after Suez as the context for the retreat from Africa that culminated in the 1960 “Wind of Change” speech. In it Macmillan never invoked Suez and framed African nationalism as a Cold War reality Britain had to “come to terms with.” Even so, the speech’s logic reflects a post-Suez recognition of Britain’s reduced weight. Suez destroyed the illusion that Europe could contain African liberation movements by force, and it left Cairo a symbol of Europe’s defeat. Seventy years on, Suez remains one of the illustrations of how empires actually end: Not in a single battle, but when their own governments discover the limits of their power. Within six years of the last Anglo-French troops leaving Port Said, Ghana, Nigeria and most of France’s sub-Saharan colonies had won independence, and Algeria followed in 1962 after a war Paris could no longer afford to win. Read more Russia helps Africa become stronger – Nasser’s grandson Egypt did not cause all of this, but it gave Africa a powerful example of a post-colonial state that had defied two European powers and survived. The lesson cut both ways, however. Within weeks of the withdrawal Washington, which had forced the retreat, was preparing the Eisenhower Doctrine to fill the vacuum London and Paris left behind. What Suez ended was not Western power in the region but the era in which Britain and France could exercise it alone. For Africa and the Arab world, that opened the real contest over sovereignty, one that is still being fought today.

items.title: European Parliament would back UK rejoining the EU, says senior lawmaker
items.author: Esther Webber, Jon Stone
items.preview: Sandro Gozi, chair of the EU delegation to the U.K. parliament, says Brexit was a "disaster."
items.content: LONDON — The European Parliament would give its backing to the U.K. reentering the EU, a senior MEP said Monday ahead of a major speech by Andy Burnham on Britain’s future relationship with Europe. Sandro Gozi, chair of the EU delegation to the U.K. parliament, told POLITICO that a majority of MEPs would be in favor, adding that the European Parliament “is the institution which is the most advanced in pushing for a new kind of relationship.” He said this is the case “across the political groups” because “even the extreme right must take stock of the fact that it [Brexit] was a bad decision.” Gozi, who is visiting London to attend an annual summit of British and EU lawmakers, welcomed Burnham’s decision to reopen the debate over Brexit, describing the U.K.’s departure from the bloc as a “disaster.” He said that if the U.K. were to rejoin the EU, it would be “a victory of the progressive forces against nationalism,” finding expression in National Rally in France and the AfD in Germany. It would show that “the future is not going back to nationalistic borders, but building up a future together,” he added. Marsha de Cordova, chair of the U.K. delegation to the European Parliament, hailed Friday’s EU-U.K. summit as “the first step” towards finding a way forward in Britain’s relationship with the EU. She shrugged off criticism that Burnham has opened up new splits in the Labour Party and the Cabinet, saying that while some Labour MPs have “sensitivities” about moving closer to the EU, “the prime minister and the foreign secretary are right to want to seek to have that conversation and that dialogue and debate.” “I welcome it because the evidence is there,” she added. “We didn’t have the evidence six years ago, or even 10 years ago. But now we do have the evidence. We’ve seen what happens.” Both politicians were skeptical of the value of the Labour Party’s “red lines”— which were introduced in the 2024 election manifesto and rule out rejoining the EU, the single market, the customs union or restoring freedom of movement — which Burnham has signaled he is not yet ready to tear up. “The red lines are being swept away by the debate,” said Gozi. “For me, they they are not there anymore.” De Cordova noted the red lines were drawn up “at a very, very different time… naturally, you need to revisit those at some point.” The prime minister, who fired the starting gun on a debate about the EU in his party conference speech in September, will give a speech Monday night where he is expected to argue the U.K. has “lost more than we gained” from leaving the European Union. At the same time, he will reiterate his commitment to Labour’s red lines for the time being, as a sign of a more gradual approach. His speech comes ahead of Friday’s meeting in Brussels, where the two sides are aiming to land a series of deals on agri-food, youth mobility and electricity trading.

items.title: N100m damages: Appeal Court reserves SERAP’s case for judgment
items.author: Nwafor
items.preview: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri ABUJA – A special panel of the Court of Appeal in Abuja on Monday reserved its judgment on two separate appeals seeking to set aside a verdict that ordered the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) to pay N100 million in damages for defami
items.content: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri ABUJA – A special panel of the Court of Appeal in Abuja on Monday reserved its judgment on two separate appeals seeking to set aside a verdict that ordered the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) to pay N100 million in damages for defaming two Department of State Services (DSS) officials. The three-member panel, led by Justice Danlami Senchi, reserved the matter for judgment after all the parties adopted their final briefs of argument. The two appeals, marked CA/ABJ/CV/1114/2026 and CA/ABJ/CV/1105/2026, were filed by SERAP and its Deputy Director, Mr. Kolawole Oluwadare, respectively. While the appellants, represented by Mr. Paul Mgbenwa and Mr. Oluwatosin Adesioye, prayed for the appeals to be upheld and the High Court’s order set aside, the respondents’ legal team, led by Mr. Akinolu Kehinde, SAN, sought the dismissal of the appeals for want of merit. The Justice Senchi-led panel said it would communicate the judgment date to the parties. It will be recalled that a High Court of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), in a judgment delivered on May 5, awarded damages against SERAP and Mr. Oluwadare, who were sued as the 1st and 2nd defendants. The trial judge, Justice Yusuf Halilu, held that he was satisfied that the non-governmental organisation had, on September 9, 2024, tarnished the reputations of two DSS personnel, Sarah John and Gabriel Ogundele, when it falsely alleged that they had invaded its office in Abuja. The court held that the defendants had unjustly defamed the operatives when they published on SERAP’s website and X (formerly Twitter) handle that the operatives had invaded the office and harassed a staff member. According to the court, the publication was in bad taste. Therefore, in addition to the N100m damages, the court ordered SERAP to tender public apologies to the defamed DSS operatives in two national newspapers, on two television stations and on its website. It also ordered the defendants to pay the two operatives N1m to cover the cost of the litigation, as well as 10 per cent annual interest on the judgment sum until it is fully liquidated. The judgment followed Suit No. CV/4547/2024, which the two operatives filed before the court to challenge what they regarded as SERAP’s false claim, which had negatively affected both their reputations and the corporate image of the DSS. The appellants are asking the court to set aside the judgment in its entirety, insisting that the trial judge erred in law and occasioned a miscarriage of justice against them. In processes filed through its lawyers, led by Mr. Tayo Oyetibo, SAN, SERAP anchored its appeal on 24 grounds. It raised questions concerning the essential elements of defamation, the evidential burden of establishing identification, the competence of the evidence relied upon by the trial court, and the protection of freedom of expression and public-interest advocacy. “The central issue in this appeal is whether the respondents established by credible evidence that the publications complained of referred to them. The publications did not name the respondents, and the descriptions relied upon were general physical descriptions which did not, without more, identify the particular individuals who brought the action. “The alleged suspension of the 1st and 2nd Respondents was likewise not supported by independent documentary evidence. The award against SERAP was therefore not only excessive but also arbitrary and ought to be set aside. “The award of liability cannot stand where the essential findings on falsity and justification were not supported by the evidence. We respectfully submit that the finding of liability and consequential award of damages cannot stand once the findings upon which they were founded are shown to be erroneous. “Where a claimant is not expressly named in a publication, the burden remains on the claimant to establish by evidence the circumstances from which a reasonable reader would understand the publication to refer specifically to that claimant. That essential link was not established in this case. “Neither publication identified the respondents by name, rank, designation, office or photograph. The descriptions relied upon were physical descriptions which, on the evidence before the trial court, were not unique to the respondents. “The respondents pleaded that members of the public and persons within the SSS understood the publications to refer to them, but no member of the public was called to testify that they had read the publications and understood them to refer to the respondents. “No independent witness was called to establish the alleged identification, while the social-media reactions relied upon by the respondents were not tendered in evidence. “The law is settled that the words complained of in an action for defamation must be considered from the standpoint of the ordinary reasonable reader. The question is whether a reasonable person reading the publication would associate the words complained of with the claimant. “The significance of this principle in the present appeal is considerable. The two SSS/DSS officers were not named in either publication. Their case therefore depended upon establishing by evidence the factual circumstances connecting the descriptions contained in the publications to their particular identities. “The trial court consequently supplied the missing identifying link by relying, among other things, on its own observation of the physical appearance of the respondents in court. “The trial court could not properly supply by its own observation the essential identifying link which the respondents were required to establish by evidence. “The issue was whether the publications identified the respondents when they were published, not whether the respondents happened to fit the descriptions when they appeared before the court,” SERAP argued. The post N100m damages: Appeal Court reserves SERAP’s case for judgment appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.content: Greene Da’monte Khiree allegedly abandoned two bags containing nearly 34 kg of marijuana after arriving from Thailand, officials have said Nigerian anti-narcotics authorities have arrested an American professional basketball player after they say they discovered nearly 34 kg of cannabis in two bags he abandoned at Lagos international airport. The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said on Sunday that Greene Da’monte Khiree, 28, arrived at Murtala Muhammed International Airport on November 11 aboard an Emirates flight from Thailand via Dubai. Acting on intelligence about the shipment, officers placed him under surveillance and observed him leaving his checked bags behind and attempting to exit with only his carry-on luggage, the agency said. “He was promptly apprehended at the airport car park,” it added. Investigators found 32 parcels containing 33.95 kg of ‘Loud’, which the NDLEA described as a potent cannabis strain, in bags bearing his name tags. A tracking device was also recovered. The suspect, from Savannah in the US state of Georgia, told investigators he had lived in Thailand since October 2025, playing professional basketball, and was visiting Nigeria on holiday to develop career contacts. The agency said a forensic examination of his phone indicated his knowledge of and involvement in the alleged trafficking operation. READ MORE: Nigeria busts Mexican-linked meth cartel Basketball outlet BasketNews said Greene’s career included spells with the Georgia Bombers and clubs in Thailand. Nigeria is a production, transit, and destination hub for illicit drugs, according to the 2025 Africa Organized Crime Index. Despite the authorities destroying cannabis plantations, traffickers continue to move the drug into and out of the country, while locally produced methamphetamine is exported to international markets. Read more This continent is fighting to refine its own oil. Can its richest man help? In its statement on Sunday, the NDLEA also said it arrested a Nigerian, Chinedu Onwude, 56, at Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos on November 11 after finding 25.05 kg of methamphetamine hidden in breakfast cereal packs. The agency said he had returned from South Africa, where he had lived for more than 24 years under the assumed name Omokan Isaac Babatope. In May, the NDLEA announced the dismantling of a Mexican-linked methamphetamine cartel in Ogun and Lagos states, arresting ten suspects, including three Mexican nationals. Officials reported recovering more than 2.4 metric tons of drugs, precursor chemicals, and industrial solvents. Last November, the agency reported finding 1,000 kg of cocaine at Tincan Island Port in Lagos and said it was working with US and British counterparts to identify the cartel behind the shipment.

items.title: Iyovwaye challenges Oborevwori over Adeda’s death, Asaba rally violence
items.author: Nwafor
items.preview: By Egufe Yafugborhi ASABA — Governorship candidate of the New Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Delta State, Chris Iyovwaye, has challenged Governor Sheriff Oborevwori to provide an update on the investigation into the death of late Deputy Director, Unity Adeda, before demandi
items.content: By Egufe Yafugborhi ASABA — Governorship candidate of the New Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Delta State, Chris Iyovwaye, has challenged Governor Sheriff Oborevwori to provide an update on the investigation into the death of late Deputy Director, Unity Adeda, before demanding the prosecution of suspects involved in the November 7 violence at an NDC rally in Asaba. Iyovwaye, in a statement, questioned what he described as differing levels of urgency by the state government in addressing the two incidents, insisting that Deltans deserved accountability in both cases. He said the government’s call for the prosecution of those involved in the Asaba rally violence should also extend to anyone who might have acted under government authority. “The Delta State Government has called for prosecution over the violence at the NDC rally in Asaba. We expect that investigation to examine the conduct of anyone who may have acted under government authority. “Governor, you must also speak to Deltans about the death of Mr Unity Adeda. What has the investigation established about the circumstances of his death? “What is the status of those arrested, including your Commissioner for Secondary Education? Have charges been filed? “We demand a public update and the prosecution of anyone against whom the evidence supports charges, regardless of office,” he said. The NDC candidate also questioned reported remarks by the Commissioner for Information, Charles Aniagwu, concerning a tricycle task force allegedly linked to the Asaba incident. He urged Oborevwori to clarify the identities of the task force members, who appointed and deployed them, the instructions they received and those responsible for supervising their activities. “Commissioner Charles Aniagwu’s reported remarks about a tricycle task force raise questions that Governor Sheriff Oborevwori must answer publicly. “What are the names of the task force members that were involved? Who appointed them, who deployed them, what instructions did they receive, and who supervised them?” he asked. Iyovwaye said the investigation should establish whether public authority or resources were deployed against NDC supporters, stressing that membership of a government-appointed task force did not confer the right to assault citizens or intimidate political supporters. Citing Sections 33 and 40 of the Nigerian Constitution, he said the rights to life, peaceful assembly and association must be protected irrespective of political affiliation. He also alleged that NDC banners, posters and other campaign materials had been destroyed across the state, calling on the police to investigate possible involvement of public officials or government-appointed agents. “Governor Oborevwori should publicly direct every state task force to stay within its mandate and stop any interference with lawful political activity,” he said. Warning public employees and political appointees against carrying out unlawful directives, Iyovwaye said that instructions from superiors could not excuse illegal actions. “A superior’s order cannot make an unlawful act lawful,” he declared. He maintained that the NDC would not be intimidated, claiming that residents dissatisfied with APC leadership at different levels were supporting his party. “The NDC will not be intimidated. Across Delta State, people who are tired of APC leadership at every level are standing with us. “We will continue to organise peacefully and defend the right of every Deltan to support the party of their choice,” he said. Iyovwaye urged residents to hold the governor and his administration accountable, insisting that the government’s condemnation of the Asaba rally violence must be followed by concrete measures to protect citizens participating in political gatherings. items.title: Asake, Wizkid, Burna Boy, Davido, nominated for 2027 Grammys
items.author: Ayobami
items.preview: Nigerian music star Tems leads the Nigerian nominees with four nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards, while Asake, Wizkid, Burna Boy, Davido and Ayra Starr also earned nods across African music, global music and R&B categories. The post Asake, Wizkid, Burna Boy, Davido, nominate
items.content: By Adegboyega Adeleye Nigerian music star Tems leads the Nigerian nominees with four nominations for the 2027 Grammy Awards, while Asake, Wizkid, Burna Boy, Davido and Ayra Starr also earned nods across African music, global music and R&B categories. The nominations were announced on Monday during a live YouTube programme, as the Recording Academy unveiled nominees across 100 categories ahead of the awards ceremony. Tems leads the Nigerian nominees with four nominations. She is nominated for Best R&B Song and Best R&B Solo Performance for “What You Need.” In the solo performance category, she will compete against Beyoncé for “Morning Dew (Donk),” Kehlani for “Out the Window,” Victoria Monét for “Let Me” and Jill Scott for “Pressha.” Tems is also nominated for Best African Music Performance for “Big Daddy” and Best Global Music Album for Love Is a Kingdom. “What You Need” was released on 21 November 2025 as a single from her EP Love Is a Kingdom. Asake is nominated for Best African Music Performance for “Gratitude” and shares another nomination in the category with Wizkid for their collaboration “Jogodo.” Other nominees include Tems for “Big Daddy,” and Ayra Starr and Angélique Kidjo for “Aye Kan (Are You Coming Back?),” as well as King Ayisoba featuring Rocky Dawuni for “No Tradition, No Africa.” Wizkid’s nomination comes through “Jogodo,” his collaboration with Asake, in the Best African Music Performance category. Burna Boy is nominated alongside Shakira for “Dai Dai” in the Best Global Music Performance category. Davido is nominated for Best Global Music Album for Oriadé. The category also features Anitta’s Equilibrivm, Angélique Kidjo’s Hope!!, Ayra Starr’s Starrgirl and Tems’ Love Is a Kingdom. Ayra Starr has two nominations: Best African Music Performance with Angélique Kidjo for “Aye Kan (Are You Coming Back?)” and Best Global Music Album for Starrgirl. The 69th Grammy Awards are scheduled to hold on 7 February 2027 at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, California. items.title: Shaun Tait, Kusal Mendis want extra push for Pakistan-Sri Lanka series result
items.author: none@none.com (AFP)
items.preview: Sri Lankan skipper Kusal Mendis and Pakistan bowling coach Shaun Tait urged their teams to push hard for a result in the second and final Test starting on Tuesday in Rawalpindi. A combination of bad weather and less penetrative bowling on a seemingly grassy pitch left the first T
items.content: Sri Lankan skipper Kusal Mendis and Pakistan bowling coach Shaun Tait urged their teams to push hard for a result in the second and final Test starting on Tuesday in Rawalpindi. A combination of bad weather and less penetrative bowling on a seemingly grassy pitch left the first Test without a result. Sri Lanka twice spurned chances to force a result as they let go a strong position of 404-4 in reply to Pakistan’s 434-9 declared, slumping to 446 all out. They then had Pakistan 57-3 on the final day before dropping crucial catches as the hosts closed the match on 284-8. Kusal said his team wanted to put pressure on Pakistan. “We were looking to establish a decent lead to put pressure on the Pakistan but credit must go to Saqib Khan, who bowled exceptionally well and restricted us,” said Kusal. Kusal and Dhananjaya de Silva hit hundreds and added 249 for the fifth wicket, but Sri Lanka lost their last six wickets for a mere 42 runs. It was Saqib who derailed Sri Lanka with figures of 7-130, becoming the fourth Pakistani to take seven wickets on debut. Kusal said the wicket for the second Test is green. “The wicket looks quite green and has similarities to the surface we played on in the first Test so we will assess the conditions before making a final decision.” Sri Lanka may be tempted to bring one from spinners Prabath Jayasuriya or Keshara Nuwantha. Pakistan is considering handing Test cap to rookie 19-year-old pacer Ali Shabbir for Razaullah. Tait hoped Pakistan players would make an extra effort to win their first Test series this year. “That extra push is needed,” said Tait, a former Australian pacer. “I am happy with the way bowlers bowled during the majority of the last Test and want some extra push.” Experienced batter Saud Shakeel missed centuries in both innings with scores of 93 and 97. Skipper Babar Azam’s Test century drought continued with 42 innings without a three-figure knock. The two-match series is part of the World Test Championship’s fourth cycle, with Pakistan (ninth and last) and Sri Lanka (seventh) already out of next year’s final.

items.content: فرانسيسكا موسى لا يقتصر تأثير غياب الشمس على تغيّر الطقس وقصر ساعات النهار، بل قد يمتدّ إلى ما هو أبعد من ذلك، ليطال توازننا النفسي وقدراتنا الذهنية. فمع دخول فصل الشتاء وتراجع التعرّض للضوء الطبيعي، قد يختلّ إيقاع الساعة البيولوجية، وتتأثر جودة النوم ومستويات الطاقة، فيما تظهر انعكاسات محتملة على المزاج و الذاكرة والتركيز. وبين الإرهاق المتزايد، والتشتّت الذهني، وتقلبات الحالة النفسية، يبرز سؤال أساسي: إلى أي مدى يمكن لقلّة التعرّض لأشعة الشمس أن تؤثر في صحتنا النفسية ووظائفنا الإدراكية، ومتى تتحوّل هذه التغيّرات الموسمية من حالة عابرة إلى مؤشرات تستدعي الانتباه؟ قلة الضوء واضطراب الساعة البيولوجية مع حلول الشتاء وتراجع ساعات التعرّض لضوء الشمس، قد لا يكون التغيير موسمياً فحسب، بل يمتدّ ليطال المزاج والطاقة والقدرات الذهنية. تشرح الاختصاصية النفسية دنيا عيّاد أنّ ضوء الشمس يؤدي دوراً أساسياً في تنظيم الساعة البيولوجية للجسم، أي النظام المسؤول عن ضبط مواعيد النوم والاستيقاظ والتكيّف مع تعاقب الليل والنهار. ومع تراجع التعرّض للضوء الطبيعي، قد يواجه بعض الأشخاص اضطرابات في النوم، وزيادة في الشعور بالإرهاق، وانخفاضاً في مستويات النشاط والانتباه. وتنعكس هذه التغيّرات بدورها على قدرة معالجة المعلومات وتنظيم الأفكار والتركيز، ما قد يُفسَّر أحياناً على أنّه ضعف في الذاكرة، فيما يكون مرتبطاً بالإجهاد واضطراب النوم وتراجع الانتباه. كذلك، قد تظهر تقلّبات في المزاج ، وفقدان الاهتمام بأنشطة اعتاد الشخص الاستمتاع بها. وتشير عيّاد إلى أنّ بعض هذه الأعراض قد يرتبط بالاكتئاب الموسمي، الذي يظهر غالباً خلال أشهر الشتاء، وقد يترافق مع التعب وزيادة النوم وصعوبة التركيز والانسحاب الاجتماعي. لكنها تؤكد أنّ الشعور بالحزن أو التعب لا يعني بالضرورة الإصابة بالاكتئاب، إذ تختلف الاستجابة لقلة الضوء من شخص إلى آخر تبعاً لعوامل نفسية وبيولوجية. #Analysis# روتين يومي للحدّ من التأثيرات الموسمية لا يقتصر التعامل مع تأثيرات تبدّل الفصول على انتظار عودة الطقس الدافئ، بل يبدأ باتخاذ خطوات يومية تساعد على الحفاظ على التوازن النفسي والجسدي. تنصح عيّاد بالحفاظ على التعرّض لضوء النهار قدر الإمكان، والالتزام بمواعيد منتظمة للنوم والاستيقاظ، لما لذلك من أهمية في تنظيم الساعة البيولوجية . كما تشدّد على ضرورة المحافظة على النشاط اليومي، وممارسة الأنشطة التي تمنح الشخص شعوراً بالراحة، وتعزيز التواصل الاجتماعي. وتلفت إلى أهمية مراقبة أي تغيّرات مستمرة في الحالة النفسية، ولا سيما انخفاض المزاج، والإرهاق، وفقدان الرغبة في ممارسة الأنشطة المعتادة أو الاختلاط بالآخرين. وفي حال استمرار هذه الأعراض أو تأثيرها على الحياة اليومية، توصي عيّاد بطلب المساعدة من اختصاصي نفسي لتقييم الحالة والتعامل معها بالشكل المناسب. فالتغيّرات التي يفرضها تبدّل الفصول ليست دائماً عابرة، وفهم تأثيرها في الصحة النفسية والذهنية هو الخطوة الأولى للتعامل معها بوعي.

items.title: Marine Corps doubles, extends contract for M27 rifles
items.author: Daniel Terrill
items.preview: The service began replacing its infantry’s squad weapons with the M27 IAR in 2028 and will continue through 2028.
items.content: The Marine Corps more than doubled the contract ceiling with gunmaker Heckler & Koch for the M27 Infantry Automatic Rifle, or IAR. According to the Nov. 6 notice , the contract value increased by $45.4 million, a jump from $39.23 million to $84.6 million. That price covers new guns, parts and associated equipment. The notice came roughly eight months after the service revealed that it opted to keep the M27 rather than adopting the Army’s higher-caliber M7 rifle . In February, a Marine Corps spokesperson explained to Military Times that the M27 was better suited “for our close combat formations” and aligned with its service requirements. Although the Marine Corps has tested and fielded the M27 for more than 15 years, the service expanded use of the weapon system in 2018 with a five-year contract for indefinite delivery/indefinite quantity, or IDIQ. Although the M27 is the Marine Corps’ current service weapon for all infantry battalions, it was originally only meant to replace the M249 Squad Automatic Weapon, or SAW. However, because of its size, capabilities, and reliability, the service made it standard issue for the infantry, replacing the legacy M4A1 and M16A4 systems. In 2018, Marine Corps spokesmen explained said the M27 provides “the necessary increase in lethality” as the weapon system “has proven to be the best overall fighting rifle” and they predicted “an immediate increase in overall combat capability.” Like its predecessors, the M27 is chambered for 5.56mm NATO rounds and is can use the same 30-round magazine. Modeled after the HK416 — the weapon used to kill Osama bin Laden — the M27 uses a short-stroke gas-piston operating system, but it features a barrel at 16.5 inches. The longer barrel gives the M27 greater range. Since fielding the M27, the service has also adopted new standard equipment like suppressors and lasers as well as capabilities for the platform. Earlier this year, Marines began new service-level training to shoot down small unmanned aerial systems, or sUASs (aka drones), with the M27 and other small arms. According to the notice, Heckler & Koch will continue to supply the service with the M27 through April 2028. Most of the manufacturing will occur at the gunmaker’s facility in Oberndorf, Germany, and the rest in Columbus, Georgia.

items.content: The Marine Corps more than doubled the contract ceiling with gunmaker Heckler & Koch for the M27 Infantry Automatic Rifle, or IAR. According to the Nov. 6 notice , the contract value increased by $45.4 million, a jump from $39.23 million to $84.6 million. That price covers new guns, parts and associated equipment. The notice came roughly eight months after the service revealed that it opted to keep the M27 rather than adopting the Army’s higher-caliber M7 rifle . In February, a Marine Corps spokesperson explained to Military Times that the M27 was better suited “for our close combat formations” and aligned with its service requirements. Although the Marine Corps has tested and fielded the M27 for more than 15 years, the service expanded use of the weapon system in 2018 with a five-year contract for indefinite delivery/indefinite quantity, or IDIQ. Although the M27 is the Marine Corps’ current service weapon for all infantry battalions, it was originally only meant to replace the M249 Squad Automatic Weapon, or SAW. However, because of its size, capabilities, and reliability, the service made it standard issue for the infantry, replacing the legacy M4A1 and M16A4 systems. In 2018, Marine Corps spokesmen explained said the M27 provides “the necessary increase in lethality” as the weapon system “has proven to be the best overall fighting rifle” and they predicted “an immediate increase in overall combat capability.” Like its predecessors, the M27 is chambered for 5.56mm NATO rounds and is can use the same 30-round magazine. Modeled after the HK416 — the weapon used to kill Osama bin Laden — the M27 uses a short-stroke gas-piston operating system, but it features a barrel at 16.5 inches. The longer barrel gives the M27 greater range. Since fielding the M27, the service has also adopted new standard equipment like suppressors and lasers as well as capabilities for the platform. Earlier this year, Marines began new service-level training to shoot down small unmanned aerial systems, or sUASs (aka drones), with the M27 and other small arms. According to the notice, Heckler & Koch will continue to supply the service with the M27 through April 2028. Most of the manufacturing will occur at the gunmaker’s facility in Oberndorf, Germany, and the rest in Columbus, Georgia.

items.title: Only 14 states pay pensions regularly – PenCom
items.author: Nwafor
items.preview: The National Pension Commission (PenCom) has disclosed that only 14 of Nigeria’s 36 states are meeting their pension obligations regularly, raising concerns over persistent delays in the payment of retirement benefits by several state governments. The Director-General of PenCom,
items.content: The National Pension Commission (PenCom) has disclosed that only 14 of Nigeria’s 36 states are meeting their pension obligations regularly, raising concerns over persistent delays in the payment of retirement benefits by several state governments. The Director-General of PenCom, Omolola Oloworaran, disclosed this during an interview with ARISE NEWS on Monday, acknowledging that some states were performing poorly in meeting their pension obligations to retirees. “We have 14 states that are paying up. But 14 out of 36 states is a lot. And some states are doing very badly,” she said. Oloworaran, however, did not identify the states making regular payments or those defaulting on their pension obligations. On the Federal Government’s minimum pension initiative, the PenCom chief disclosed that the ₦400bn provided by the Federal Government and the pension industry for the Pension Protection Fund could sustain the programme for at least 10 years based on current projections. She explained that the Federal Government contributed ₦350bn, while the pension industry provided ₦50bn. According to her, the commission had engaged an actuary to assess the financial requirements of the initiative and determine its long-term sustainability. “Conservatively, we’re good for the next 10 years. Conservatively,” she said. She, however, noted that the projections could be reviewed in response to inflation and the funds available to support the programme. Oloworaran assured that the commission remained committed to ensuring that vulnerable retirees continued to receive financial support under the minimum pension arrangement. She further disclosed that the Pension Protection Fund had a balance of ₦38bn before the current administration, adding that part of the Federal Government’s contribution was intended to clear outstanding pension backlogs. She said 54 per cent of beneficiaries who had received payments under the initiative were private-sector retirees, while nearly 70 per cent of workers expected to qualify for the programme were also from the private sector. Police pension dispute On the controversy surrounding retired police officers seeking to exit the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS) and return to the Defined Benefit Scheme (DBS), Oloworaran said PenCom was working with the police to develop an arrangement that would safeguard their retirement savings. She disclosed that different options had been presented to President Bola Tinubu for consideration, stressing that the priority was to ensure improved pension benefits for police retirees without jeopardising their funds. “But what we want to do is put a structure in place. Where we are sure that nothing at all will happen to the funds for our police,” she said. According to her, the ultimate objective was to ensure that retired police officers received higher pension benefits, irrespective of the arrangement eventually adopted. “And the ultimate result is more money in the hands of police. Whether you do it in the scheme or outside the scheme, it doesn’t matter,” she added. The PenCom chief expressed optimism that the dispute would be resolved before the end of the year, although she acknowledged that bureaucratic processes could delay the outcome. “I’m hoping, I mean, government is tough. A lot of bureaucracy here and there. I’m hoping before the end of the year, we would have resolved the police issue,” she said. President Tinubu had on November 10, 2026, launched the ₦52,500 monthly minimum pension guarantee for 173,209 eligible retirees under the Contributory Pension Scheme, ending a 22-year delay in implementing the provision of the Pension Reform Act. He also inaugurated the Pension Industry Healthcare Plan for Retirees (PenCare), designed to provide free essential healthcare services to low-income pensioners. The initiatives were unveiled at a ceremony in Abuja, where the President was represented by Senate President Godswill Akpabio. items.content: اعتبر الكرملين الاثنين أنّ القمة المرتقبة بين الرئيس الروسي فلاديمير بوتين ونظيره الصيني شي جينبينغ والأميركي دونالد ترامب هذا الأسبوع، هي على قدر من الأهمية والرمزية. وقال مستشار بوتين للسياسة الخارجية يوري أوشاكوف للصحافيين قبل القمة التي تعقد الخميس في مدينة شنجن الصينية، إنه "يصعب المبالغة في تقدير أهمية ورمزية هذا الاجتماع". وأشار الى أن الاجتماع يستند الى صيغة تأخذ في الاعتبار "التفاهم المتبادل والتحالف بين بلداننا خلال الحرب العالمية الثانية". وتخشى دول أوروبية، إضافة الى أوكرانيا التي تواجه غزوا روسياً منذ العام 2022، أن تسعى موسكو عبر هذه القمة الاستثنائية، الى الدفع نحو "يالطا جديدة"، في إشارة الى اجتماع تاريخي بين الاتحاد السوفياتي والولايات المتحدة والمملكة المتحدة في شبه جزيرة القرم عام 1945، تقاسمت بموجبه هذه الأطراف النفوذ في القارة، ما مهّد الأرضية لحقبة الحرب الباردة. وأعلنت بكين الاثنين أن الرؤساء الثلاثة سيبحثون "السلام العالمي" خلال أول قمة ثلاثية لهم في شنجن. ولم تقدّم الصين تفاصيل كثيرة عن المواضيع التي سيناقشها الرؤساء الثلاثة، لكن المتحدثة باسم وزارة الخارجية ماو نينغ أوضحت أنهم سيجرون "حواراً معمقاً بشأن صون السلام العالمي وتعزيز الاستقرار الاستراتيجي في العلاقات بين القوى الكبرى"، معتبرة أن اللقاء "سيحمل أهمية تاريخية".
