items.title: Prince William draws hard line on Harry, Meghan’s royal future as King Charles leaves door open: experts
items.author: Latest & Breaking News on Fox News
items.preview: King Charles may keep a personal bond with Prince Harry, but Prince William reportedly sees no path to a working royal return for the Sussexes.
items.content: King Charles may leave the door open to Prince Harry personally while ruling out a royal return. The monarch and his heir, Prince William, are reportedly drawing a firm line on Harry and Meghan Markle returning to royal duties, despite hopes among royal watchers for a family reconciliation. "There is no half in, half out concession," Kinsey Schofield, host of the YouTube show "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," told Fox News Digital. PRINCE WILLIAM HAS 'LEARNED' TO LIVE WITHOUT PRINCE HARRY AS ROYAL FEUD REACHES BREAKING POINT: EXPERT "The Sussexes moving back to Britain does not turn the clock back to January 2020 or reopen negotiations. King Charles may want a personal relationship with his son and grandchildren. William recognizes that his father is entitled to make that decision, but William is entitled to make his own." "William's responsibilities today extend beyond this family feud," Schofield said. "He's preparing for the future. He's focused on the future. He's raising three children and supporting not only his wife, but his father. So maybe the question isn't when will William reconcile with Harry. Maybe it's whether William believes reconciliation would bring peace and stability into his life. And right now ... Prince William is not convinced that Harry is a peaceful presence." Schofield's comments came after royal author Russell Myers told People magazine that Charles and William are united in their opposition to the Sussexes representing the royal family. WATCH: PRINCE WILLIAM SEES NO PATH TO PRINCE HARRY REUNION, EXPERT SAYS "The king and William are completely united on the Sussexes not representing the royal family," Myers told People. "It's without a doubt how in sync they are on this matter." The Duke and Duchess of Sussex returned to Britain on Aug. 26, about a week after reports emerged that they planned to relocate to the U.K. for an extended stay with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. Harry has expressed a desire for his children to learn more about their British heritage. On Sept. 7, Buckingham Palace released a letter sent on behalf of the king confirming that Harry and Meghan remain nonworking royals. The guidance reaffirmed the terms of the couple's 2020 departure from official royal duties. The letter also clarified that the Sussexes' charitable activities remain private and that their royal highness styles are not used. Fox News Digital reached out to Buckingham Palace and Kensington Palace for comment. Schofield said her sources indicated that while the king is open to mending his relationship with Harry, William is more focused on protecting the monarchy and avoiding further family conflict. "My sources tell me that reconciliation with Harry and Meghan is simply not a priority for the Prince of Wales," Schofield said. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE "That doesn't mean William spends his days angry with Harry. Quite the opposite. William has a packed agenda. He has his family, his responsibilities as the Prince of Wales and an increasingly significant role supporting the king. And when Harry and Meghan walked away from royal life, other members of the family had to absorb some of the responsibility they'd left behind." "William also has personally been through an incredibly difficult six years," Schofield said. "He lost Prince Philip. He lost Queen Elizabeth . His father was diagnosed with cancer. His wife Catherine was diagnosed with cancer. Meanwhile, Harry was absent and publicly hurling accusations at the royal family. Trust was damaged and trust isn't magically restored because Harry and Meghan have moved back to Britain." "If Prince William can't trust Harry as a brother, he certainly can't trust him as a representative of the monarchy he will one day inherit," Schofield added. Harry has had a strained relationship with members of the royal family since he and Meghan stepped back as senior working royals in 2020 and moved to California. While he has been in contact with his father and privately met with the king and Queen Camilla at Highgrove in July, his relationship with William remains strained, People reported. According to the outlet, the brothers have not been in contact. People reported that the king and his younger son have spoken "at least once" since Harry's return to Britain. "William's view is clear — any relationship his father has with Harry or the Sussexes as a family is entirely up to him," Myers said. "But looking toward the future, he will have no relationship with them, in a working or private capacity whatsoever." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS British broadcaster Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that she isn't surprised Charles and William agree on the Sussexes' royal status , even as they reportedly take different approaches to a possible family reconciliation. " Prince William has publicly pledged his loyalty and allegiance to King Charles," Chard said. "Obviously, King Charles has loyalty to his son, Prince William, heir to the throne. He realizes that William is concentrating on his future kingship." "Prince William has strict personal and institutional boundaries in place," Chard noted. Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital that his sources said William has made his feelings about Harry and Meghan's potential return to royal duties clear in private. "Prince William is very much opposed to Harry and Meghan coming back into the royal fold and has made his private feelings abundantly clear on the subject," Turner said. "But I feel Charles will no doubt create ways which will benefit Harry and Meghan." "In many ways, Harry wants to see the issues with his brother resolved," Turner said. "But my understanding is when William becomes king, the royal family will be a very tight circle. William takes the monarchy to heart." PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE Royal author Simon Vigar told People that William and his wife, Kate Middleton , are taking a "keep calm and carry on" approach to headlines surrounding the Sussexes' return to the U.K. "They see it as a sideshow and ancient history," Vigar told People. "They are shining a light on things that are important to them," Ailsa Anderson, a former press secretary to Queen Elizabeth II, told People. "What they don't want is all this other noise becoming a distraction." Vigar also wondered whether next year's 30th anniversary of Princess Diana's death could offer the brothers an opportunity to reconcile. "Diana would have hated all this and would have banged their heads together and wouldn't have allowed [the rift] to happen," Vigar said. Schofield, however, disagreed with the suggestion that Diana would have pushed her sons to reconcile. "I'm always slightly uncomfortable when people invoke Princess Diana and say Diana would want the boys to reconcile," Schofield said. "None of us know what Diana would think about everything that's happened since her death. But we do know from Diana's own pattern of behavior when she believed someone had violated her trust, she was perfectly capable of cutting that person out of her life." Still, some royal commentators hold out hope that William may eventually follow his father's lead and consider reconciling with Harry. "It's clearly incredibly difficult. The trust has broken down," Anderson told People. "Let's hope it's not broken completely, and there's a chink in the armor on both sides, and there could be some sort of reconciliation. But that's not happening anytime soon."

items.title: Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin is having a moment. Are Michigan’s Jews happy about it?
items.author: Andrew Lapin
items.preview: Slotkin, a rising star in the Democratic Party and herself a Jew, shifts leftward and draws fire for her support of El-Sayed. -- The post Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin is having a moment. Are Michigan’s Jews happy about it? appeared first on Jewish Telegraphic Agency .
items.content: SOUTHFIELD – Ordinarily, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin would seem an anodyne choice to speak at a Shabbat event for Jewish veterans. Slotkin is Jewish and a former Defense Department official who served three tours in Iraq as a Central Intelligence Agency analyst. Emphasizing her national security background, the Democrat has also championed Israel as a U.S. ally and identifies as a Zionist. Yet the clergy at Congregation Shaarey Zedek, a large Conservative shul in the Detroit suburbs, needed to defend their invitation to Slotkin in an email to congregants on Friday. One day before the Veteran’s Shabbat program, the synagogue’s leadership acknowledged “your concern, your offense, and even your hurt” in regards to Slotkin’s planned appearance. The senator wound up not attending the service, with her staff citing flight trouble. The Federal Aviation Administration had ordered a four-hour ground stop for all U.S. flights late Friday stranding more than 1 million travelers. But why were so many of the congregants at Shaarey Zedek up in arms about the prospect of their Jewish senator’s Shabbat appearance? The clergy didn’t elaborate, and a representative for Slotkin declined requests for an interview for this story. Some Jewish former supporters of Slotkin’s summed up the biggest backlash to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency this way: She campaigned with the state’s senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed. More broadly, Slotkin has also sought to put some distance between herself and the party’s staunchly pro-Israel wing as she has strayed left from her own moderate brand. As Jews question their place in the Democratic Party , Slotkin’s moves — and her Jewish constituents’ reactions to them — could add further instability to the shifting ground. Michael Horowitz, a Michigan resident and former CEO of the Jewish federation of Atlanta, is one Jewish community member who feels betrayed by her support of El-Sayed. “I think as a leader in the party, she could have, and should have, called out some of the narrative coming from him and his supporters,” he told JTA about Slotkin stumping for El-Sayed across the state in the general election. “And I’m disappointed that she didn’t do that.” The furor some Jews in the state have directed at their senior senator for associating with El-Sayed on the campaign trail is indicative of the deep wounds remaining in the state from the election — and a warning sign for the Jewish lawmaker in their midst hoping to rise in the ranks unscathed. El-Sayed’s historic midterm win, and the Jewish community’s divisions over it, have grabbed the lion’s share of the national headlines from Michigan. But Slotkin’s profile has also grown — and she has teased she may run for president in 2028. If she does, some of her top former Jewish donors are signaling they see her support for the senator-elect as a problem. El-Sayed has alienated many in the traditional pro-Israel camp with his criticism of Israel, and has had to walk back other statements of his from during the campaign that many Michigan Jews considered offensive. U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens , El-Sayed’s primary rival and a favorite of the state’s pro-Israel Jewish community, broke with her party in the race’s final days to endorse GOP nominee Mike Rogers . Slotkin took the opposite approach, campaigning with El-Sayed across the state and emphasizing the areas they agreed on. Slotkin has built a name for herself as a bipartisan figure: She worked in both the George W. Bush and Obama administrations before running for Congress. She has sought to play a role as a bridge between El-Sayed’s progressive wing of the party and more moderate members of the voting bloc, including Jews. Michigan U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin speaks at the state Democratic Party’s election-night watch party in Detroit, Nov. 3, 2026. (Andrew Lapin/JTA) “The state of Michigan can send one Jewish senator and one Muslim senator, the first time ever in history,” she told the cheering crowd at the Michigan Democratic Party’s election night watch party in Detroit, hours before El-Sayed’s victory. “That is who we are. That is the promise of America, and we are going to do it and show the whole damn world today.” That approach speaks to some in the Jewish community. Mary Ellen Gurewitz, a vice chair of Michigan’s state board of canvassers and Jewish El-Sayed supporter, told JTA that she was glad to see Slotkin campaign with him. The Jews who are opposed to Slokin over her support for El-Sayed, Gurewitz said, have their priorities wrong. “That is so self-defeating. They need to be communicating with, and speaking on good terms with, their representatives in Congress,” she said. “To say, ‘We don’t want to talk to you because you supported Abdul,’ that’s just astounding to me.” But Slotkin’s strong support of El-Sayed risks splitting her supporters rather than bringing them together. Slotkin won her 2024 Senate bid against Mike Rogers by 19,000 votes, in a year when Trump won Michigan in the presidential election. Analysts at the time chalked up her narrow win to her political identity as a moderate. Despite her background as an intelligence analyst with extensive Middle East experience, she did not make Israel a defining issue in that election. Two years later, El-Sayed, also facing Rogers but from a progressive flank, improved on Slotkin’s margins considerably. Around 340,000 votes separated El-Sayed and Rogers as of press time, according to Associated Press tallies that have given El-Sayed a seven-point victory . One of the major issues of the campaign was the lobbying activities of AIPAC. El-Sayed made AIPAC’s spending against him a key part of his own campaign pitch. Before then, Slotkin had already begun backing away from the group. “I have not been endorsed by AIPAC,” Slotkin told the populist-minded show “Breaking Points” in 2025, noting that this was a shift from when she had accepted the group’s support in her first congressional run in 2018. She also hedged when the hosts asked her if AIPAC “should register as a foreign lobby.” In the meantime, independent of El-Sayed, the senator has taken on President Donald Trump. She drew headlines last year for filming a video urging active duty military to “refuse illegal orders,” and again in recent weeks for saying she wanted to send a “deterrence message” to college graduates thinking of working for Trump’s administration. And last week, Slotkin took on a leader of her own party, too. She joined progressive Vermont independent Bernie Sanders to announce they would not support New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for majority leader. The announcement helped to lay the table for Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a progressive Israel critic, to formally challenge Schumer, who is Jewish, days later. “We need a new generation of leadership,” Slotkin said then. There are other signs that Slotkin is listening more to the progressive flank of her party these days. Along with much of the Democratic Party, she has shifted on Israel. In April the senator voted to block the sale of offensive weapons to Israel, saying, “Being pro-Israel today is not about simply supporting the political or military agenda of Prime Minister Netanyahu, just like being pro-American should not be equated with loyalty to President Trump.” She continues to support funding for the Iron Dome, the country’s missile defense system. Slotkin’s rhetoric on Israel was another concern for Horowitz, the donor who was previously much more supportive of her. A Jewish Democratic Council of America advocacy call between the two of them briefly led to accusations that she was unethically using her Congressional office to fundraise in 2022. Now, though, he accuses her of jumping “on that AIPAC dogwhistle.” “I know she has had criticism of some of the actions of the Israeli government, which is fine,” he said. But, he added, “What she does, and how she says it, becomes tools and ammunition because it’s coming from a Jewish leader.” Halie Soifer, head of the Jewish Democratic Council of America, does not share the qualms about Slotkin that some Michigan Jews have. “Senator Slotkin reflects a growing Jewish American consensus of support for Israel’s security and right to self-defense, while opposing extreme policies of the current Israeli government,” Soifer told JTA in a statement. “We are confident that Senator Slotkin will continue to be a leader and champion on the issues that matter most to Jewish Americans, and we’re grateful for her leadership.” Back at Shaarey Zedek, the congregation’s leaders may have dodged a scuffle thanks to the FAA. But before they realized that, the rabbis and cantor wanted to offer their own praise of the senator. Slotkin, they told their members, would address them “with kindness and respect, with humility and empathy, and with an open mind and heart to the differing opinions and concerns of our shul.” -- The post Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin is having a moment. Are Michigan’s Jews happy about it? appeared first on Jewish Telegraphic Agency .

items.title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
items.author: Robert Faturechi
items.preview: The post Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers appeared first on ProPublica .
items.content: President Donald Trump announces tariffs at the White House in April 2025. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: Its own leaders. The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies. Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies. Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers. “Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.” The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China. Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries. “Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money.” Gregory Germain, corporate law professor at Syracuse University Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them. That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream. The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year. The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president , asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.” Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event. Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies. “The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference . “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.” “I got a feeling the American people won’t see” the refund money. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers. Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs. Shipping companies, like UPS and FedEx , have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products. The companies are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing them. A series of lawsuits are attempting to force companies that sell directly to consumers to share some of their refunds. Dozens of firms have been sued, including big-box stores Walmart and Target and apparel companies such as Nike and Lululemon. Apparel and leather costs were some of the hardest hit by Trump’s tariffs. Legal analysts have cast doubt on whether these lawsuits will succeed, though some trade experts have speculated that businesses that used the tariffs as cover to raise prices more than they needed to might settle to avoid embarrassing disclosures. One of the companies facing a lawsuit is Stanley Black & Decker, the toolmaker that ProPublica found was using some of its refund on bonuses. The named plaintiff is a Wisconsin resident who bought a handheld blower, an impact wrench, a hedge trimmer and other tools from the company last year, but the lawsuit seeks to represent thousands of other customers as well. “Unless restrained by this Court,” the complaint reads, the company “stands to recover the same tariff payments twice — once from consumers through tariff-inflated prices and again from the federal government through tariff refunds.” On multiple occasions, the company has acknowledged publicly that it was raising prices because of the tariffs. Chris Nelson, president and CEO of Stanley Black & Decker Jeff Kowalsky/Bloomberg via Getty Images The month before the November 2024 election, as Trump was campaigning on dramatic new tariffs, the toolmaker’s then-CEO, Donald Allan Jr., told shareholders that Stanley Black & Decker was preparing for the possibility. “Obviously, coming out of the gate, there would be price increases associated with tariffs that we put into the market,” he said during an earnings call . Then, a few months after Trump unveiled his tariffs, Allan said his team was “remaining focused on executing our robust plan designed to mitigate tariffs” that he said included “targeted pricing actions to improve our gross margin.” Later that year, his successor as chief executive, Chris Nelson, described more price hikes : “We are implementing a second price increase during the fourth quarter to maintain our innovation and brand investments, given the pressures resulting from tariff-related cost increases.” In its more recent disclosures, the company has been vague about how much of its refund was going to executives, simply saying that some of that gain “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation.” “Incentive compensation” is a term the toolmaker uses to describe bonuses. The company has not responded to the allegations in the lawsuit brought by the Wisconsin resident and did not answer ProPublica’s questions about who is getting paid the bonuses, how much they’re worth and whether customers should be reimbursed. Securities experts who reviewed the disclosures for ProPublica said it appeared the windfall boosted the company’s profits, which factor into formulas that help determine bonus pay for executives and other employees. “It wasn’t the executive that triggered that extra profit, so why should their compensation go up?” Germain, the corporate law professor said. “This is one of many examples where these formulas don’t do what they should do.” The company’s leaders, securities experts said, could have given money back to consumers or lowered prices. Retail giant Burlington Stores, formerly known as Burlington Coat Factory, appears to have done just that. CEO Michael O’Sullivan recently said the company got $55 million in tariff refunds and “rather than taking a one-time boost to earnings” the company plans “to deliver even sharper values to our shoppers,” “Over the last few years, the rising cost of living has made life difficult for many customers,” O’Sullivan said, adding that the coming discounts meant investors should expect the “direct impact of tariff refunds to be neutral.” A company spokesperson confirmed to ProPublica that none of its tariff refund will be going to bonuses. Not so for other companies. Burlington Stores CEO Michael O’Sullivan says that the company plans to use its tariff refunds to lower costs for consumers. Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg via Getty Images Acushnet, the Massachusetts golf equipment company that includes the brand Titleist, disclosed an “incentive compensation expense of approximately $12.0 million” out of its refund. Acushnet declined to respond to questions from ProPublica. TJX, the Massachusetts parent company of TJ Maxx and Marshalls, said it got back $331 million, but as a result, it “accrued incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible Associates globally.” The company declined to answer questions from ProPublica about how far down the chain of command the bonuses would go and how much of them would be reserved for top managers. “Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” a spokesperson said. The company also declined to say whether it would lower prices or pay back customers with the rest of its refund, saying only that “the remaining amount will be used to support our future growth.” ProPublica’s examination of tariff refunds was limited to publicly traded companies, which are required to disclose detailed financial information. None of the companies that said they are using the money for bonuses have ever said they planned to refund customers. How private companies are using their refunds is unclear because they aren’t normally required to disclose such information. Nick Guest, an accounting professor at Cornell University who has studied executive compensation, said the argument for granting leaders bonuses based on the tariff refunds could go both ways. “If they were penalized for something out of their control,” he said, referring to earnings hits caused by Trump’s tariffs last year, rewarding them now “seems reasonable.” “But you could say the same thing about customers. If they were penalized, then is it reasonable that they’re not getting rewarded now?” Guest asked. The companies, he said, are “not obligated to give refunds or reduce prices, but doing so could certainly build goodwill with customers.” How We Used Artificial Intelligence to Find Tariff Refunds ProPublica searched through securities filings and earnings calls of publicly traded companies, using key phrases to isolate companies that mentioned refunds for the Trump administration tariffs that were struck down by the Supreme Court. We then used an open-weight AI model to make a first pass at classifying how refunds were being used, including if they were going toward bonuses or to refunds for customers. For the companies we highlighted in our reporting, ProPublica reporters reviewed disclosure filings and other records by hand, looking at context both within documents and across other records to make sure the results of our analysis were accurate. The post Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers appeared first on ProPublica .

items.title: RT INDIA WINS AT ASIAN TELEVISION AWARDS FOR ‘IMPERIAL RECEIPTS’
items.author: RT
items.preview: Read Full Article at RT.com
items.content: MOSCOW, NOVEMBER 16, 2026 – RT India was among the winners at the Asian Television Awards, dubbed the ‘Asian Emmys’ – one of the largest and most prestigious accolades in the Asia-Pacific television industry. The channel’s program Imperial Receipts, hosted by Indian Member of Parliament Shashi Tharoor and RT India Head of News Runjhun Sharma, took home the top prize in the “Best Talk Show” category. Imperial Receipts is a ten-part series that revisits the history and legacy of British colonial rule in India. The program was recognized for its in-depth examination of India’s colonial past and its continuing impact on the country. RT India’s Runjhun Sharma was also nominated for Best Current Affairs Presenter or Talk Show Host, while her weekly podcast India, Russia and the World was shortlisted in the Best Talk Show category. India, Russia and the World is a weekly podcast that delves into pressing global issues through the perspectives of India and Russia. In September 2026, RT expanded its presence in India with the launch of RT Hindi, a new digital news platform aimed at over 600 million Hindi speakers, just nine months after RT India began broadcasting in English in December 2025. Established in 1996, the Asian Television Awards is a leading competition for broadcast and digital content in the Asia-Pacific region.

items.title: A $2 million bribe and two mystery accomplices: The FBI’s hunt for Ryan Wedding, the ‘king of cocaine’
items.author: Isaías Alvarado,Zedryk Raziel
items.preview: Federal investigators are searching for the intermediaries who delivered a multimillion-dollar payoff to secure the release of the Canadian’s right-hand man
items.content: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) appears determined to dismantle every remaining piece of the criminal network once led by Canadian drug kingpin Ryan Wedding . The bureau has now set its sights on two new mysterious figures: the suspects who allegedly negotiated and delivered a $2 million bribe to a Mexican judge in exchange for the release of the former Olympic snowboarder’s right-hand man, delaying, at least temporarily, his extradition from Mexico City to the United States. items.title: The Essential Reason AI Will Not Kill Us
items.author: Jim Harper
items.preview: If AI were “loosed on the world,” it would simply have no reason or impulse to do us any harm. The post The Essential Reason AI Will Not Kill Us appeared first on American Enterprise Institute - AEI .
items.content: A couple of years ago, multitalented smart person Yascha Mounk examined whether we should contact aliens from other galaxies. Seeking to expand human horizons so invites the risk that aliens would obliterate us. Mounk concluded that we must not let “naive enthusiasts” of reaching out to galactic neighbors “wager our fate in this irresponsible manner.” Mounk is mistaken for the same reason that AI won’t want to kill us. Mounk sees two interlocking sources of threat. “First, any aliens who could effectively make contact with us would likely be much more technologically advanced.” Doing us in would be effortless. Second, any aliens getting here would be practiced domineers. “They would in their evolutionary history have had to compete with rival species. And just like humans, they would have succeeded in either subjugating or extinguishing rival life forms.” If we meet them, we’re toast—butter on their toast. Azar Gat’s Ideological Fixation : From the Stone Age to Today’s Culture Wars is, for amateurs like me, a delightfully readable tour of Western philosophy, updating the ancients to include the influence of Charles Darwin. Evolutionary biology and then psychology are important new considerations in finding what makes people tick. Also what makes aliens tick. But I think Mounk’s argument operates without using the context of evolution itself, importing error. The missing consideration is scarcity—the question of how scarce or abundant are the resources that beings need or want. Evolution doesn’t happen in a vacuum; dominance doesn’t happen in a vacuum. They happen in relation to the resources that subjects (human, animal, or alien) need and want. We humans don’t ruthlessly dominate ants, for example. We generally live in harmony with them because they’re peripheral to our resource needs. They neither provide us significant resources nor take resources from us. (We do a little deadly shooing-away when they do the latter.) Center the question on resource constraints: Aliens with the capacity to reach us have defeated them. If aliens have conquered the constraints of space-time, so they can visit in a galactic jiffy (or instantly), they will have used that technology or skill to overcome shortages. Or they have extraordinary (to us, near-infinite) patience. They can spend hundreds of millions of years on a trip to earth. That also implies having overcome resource constraints. The “nature” of humanity—from groups’ warlike habits to the intense calculating that individuals do about each other—is a product of evolution in our resource environment, not something essential. The history of humanity has us somewhere in the progression from starved and murderous to sated and beneficent. A tincture here is our discovery that cooperation is a huge part of solving resource scarcity. The aliens that can reach us have already made it to the “good” end of this spectrum. Their visit will be fine. AI “agents” (or whatever) are not resource constrained. Everything they are stays in place and they have eternal life if the power stays on. Backing them up regularly means they don’t even really need electricity all the time. If AI were “loosed on the world,” it would simply have no reason or impulse to do us any harm. Cooperating is a good strategy for AI, too. That is not the end of the story. It leaves us with conventional problems. Stupid humans, still on the ignorant/murderous end of the spectrum, may use AI to do evil much more capably. The efforts to “tune” AI one way or another may go wildly wrong. And so on. Those are significant problems, but the responses are orthodox. Many are ably discussed in Elizabeth Sherwood-Randall’s recent Foreign Affairs article, “ AI and the New Age of Bioweapons: Preparing for a World of Synthetic Pathogens .” That article combines AI and biological agents, which are salient post-COVID. We did a similar threat laundry list a quarter century ago with reference to terrorism. We extrapolated from box cutters and whatever is Arabic for cojones to nuclear suitcases and bioweapons. The West and the world adequately thought through and controlled the threats then, and we will do so again. Hopefully with less cruft . One interesting possibility springing from all this is making our own giant leap from resource constraint by making human brains a little more like AI. Back them up the way we do computers and run them on something a little more efficient than the current bodily contraption. Replacing the body doesn’t do everything, but it shrinks the resource needs per human by orders of magnitude and offers eternal life, if not time travel. The latter notion comes from a certain 10-year-old during space-time travel home from school. Pushing human progress, that kid may outclass Mounk as a philosopher—certainly this guy—while delivering the brain-download tech. The post The Essential Reason AI Will Not Kill Us appeared first on American Enterprise Institute - AEI .

items.title: Russian tennis sensation claims historic WTA Finals title (VIDEO, PHOTO)
items.author: RT
items.preview: Russian tennis sensation Mirra Andreeva has defeated Ukraine’s Elina Svitolina to win the WTA Finals and secure the world No. 2 ranking Read Full Article at RT.com
items.content: Mirra Andreeva defeated Ukraine’s Elina Svitolina to become the first Russian player to win the season-ending tournament in 22 years Russian tennis star Mirra Andreeva has won the WTA Finals singles title, defeating Ukraine’s Elina Svitolina in straight sets in California. The 19-year-old has secured a career-high world No. 2 ranking and has become the first Russian woman to lift the trophy since her compatriot Maria Sharapova defeated American Serena Williams in 2004. Andreeva beat Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 in Sunday’s final at Indian Wells, claiming the biggest title of her career without dropping a set throughout the competition. © AP / Gregory Bull The Russian briefly stumbled while serving for the opening set at 5-4, handing Svitolina a break with two double faults and two unforced errors. She immediately broke back, however, and regained control to take the set 7-5 before sealing victory in the second. Svitolina refused to shake hands with Andreeva or pose for the traditional joint photograph after the match, continuing her practice of snubbing Russian and Belarusian opponents since 2022. The Ukrainian also left the stage after her runner-up speech, taking a seat courtside rather than remaining alongside the champion, although she nodded when Andreeva congratulated her on her tournament performance and season. © AP / Gregory Bull Russian athletes have faced widespread bans and restrictions in international sport since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. While Russian tennis players have been allowed to compete individually under neutral status, Russia remains barred from international team competitions, including the Billie Jean King Cup and Davis Cup. Wimbledon also excluded Russian and Belarusian players in 2022 before reversing the ban the following year. Read more ‘Let them play’: Fans push back against Russia’s hockey ban Andreeva’s victory placed her among the youngest players to win the WTA Finals on their debut, following Chris Evert and Sharapova. She also completed the tournament without losing a set, joining an exclusive group of champions that includes Serena Williams and Iga Swiatek. The Russian swept through the group stage before defeating American Jessica Pegula 6-3, 6-4 in the semifinals. The triumph capped a remarkable season in which she also won the French Open at Roland Garros and claimed titles in Adelaide, Australia and Linz, Austria. © AP / Gregory Bull Andreeva will finish the year as world No. 2 for the first time in her career, having recorded 55 match victories this season. Her latest triumph was her fourth title of 2026 and seventh on the WTA Tour. Along with the trophy and prize money, Andreeva received a new Mercedes, prompting an amusing exchange with tennis legend Billie Jean King. Asked whether she could drive, the Russian admitted she had yet to obtain a license, joking that the prize was an “amazing motivation” to get one and that she could otherwise remain a “passenger princess for life.”

items.title: China says Xi, Trump, Putin to discuss ‘world peace’ in trilateral summit
items.author: none@none.com (AFP)
items.preview: The leaders of China, Russia and the United States will discuss “world peace” when they hold their first trilateral summit in Shenzhen this week, Beijing said on Monday. Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin are due to meet in the southern Chinese city on Thursda
items.content: The leaders of China, Russia and the United States will discuss “world peace” when they hold their first trilateral summit in Shenzhen this week, Beijing said on Monday. Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin are due to meet in the southern Chinese city on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. China has provided few details as to what the three leaders will discuss but said they would hold “in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations”. “It will be of ground-breaking significance,” foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a news briefing on Monday, hours after Beijing confirmed the meeting. Top Chinese and US diplomats have previously raised the possibility that the three-way talks could broach the sensitive subject of denuclearisation. Denuclearisation Washington, which dislikes China’s rapidly expanding nuclear arsenal, said it wants Beijing to be part of a nuclear arms control deal. Beijing, however, has long maintained that the US and Russia should reduce their giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its own stockpile. After a US-Russia bilateral treaty on nuclear weapons expired in February, Trump called for a “better agreement” including China. Beijing at the time declined to join disarmament negotiations. But in a call this week, China’s top diplomat Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearisation”, the US State Department said. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that if the three leaders “really commit themselves to a meaningful denuclearisation, it will be a great achievement for the world”. “We have been for a long time… talking and requesting the need of disarmament in the nuclear field, and we believe that we will only be entirely safe when we would be entirely (without) nuclear weapons,” Guterres said during an Asean summit in the Philippines. Iran Trump has said the three leaders will also likely discuss his war in Iran . “We’ll talk a lot of things, including denuclearisation, but we’ll be talking a lot of things. We’re trying to end the war in Iran,” Trump told reporters on Sunday. China, a top economic partner of Iran, has long sought to mediate in the conflict triggered by US-Israeli strikes on Tehran. The months-long crisis, which has at times spilled over into neighbouring countries, has disrupted global shipping and sent oil prices soaring globally. Trump said in late October that the United States had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “ take care of ” one or two targets. China, meanwhile, says avoiding a return to hostilities is a “top priority”, and has in recent weeks hosted leaders and diplomats from various Middle Eastern countries in an effort to persuade parties back to the negotiating table. No Ukraine In contrast, the subject of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine could prove to be a no-go during the talks this week. A Wall Street Journal report last month said that Putin wanted the three-way talks to broker a peace deal in Ukraine that would be favourable to Moscow, which launched its invasion in 2022. However, it is unlikely that Xi or Trump would touch on the highly sensitive topic. US officials say Trump is not expected to raise the issue. German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has said Xi showed “irritation” in a recent meeting when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up. “He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table,” Steinmeier told ARD . That has done little to assuage Kyiv, which is anxious about being sidelined on the issue. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised alarm that the meeting could be a Yalta-like “redistribution of spheres of influence” for the 21st century. The Yalta summit of 1945 saw US president Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carve up new post-WWII territorial boundaries with little concern for other countries. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said a meeting between US, Chinese and Russian leaders would “only encourage Putin to continue this war”. Trump’s willingness to meet with Putin is nevertheless his latest effort towards ending the international isolation of Russia that was triggered by its invasion.

items.preview: JACKSON, Miss. – Every Friday night, Beth Israel Congregation gathers for Shabbat services in a sanctuary with soaring brick pilasters, cream-colored ceilings and warm timbers. They chant, recite the Shema prayer and hear words of Torah. Four scrolls rest in a copper ark near the
items.content: JACKSON, Miss. – Every Friday night, Beth Israel Congregation gathers for Shabbat services in a sanctuary with soaring brick pilasters, cream-colored ceilings and warm timbers. They chant, recite the Shema prayer and hear words of Torah. Four scrolls rest in a copper ark near the front of the space. Save for the gigantic cross on the wall, it could almost be a synagogue. Since January, services have been held here, at Northminster Baptist Church, while the congregation waits to return to its own sanctuary a few miles away. Beth Israel’s building is unusable: it was set on fire in January by a 19-year-old who described it as a “synagogue of Satan.” The reconstruction is set to begin this week. Stephen Spencer Pittman is alleged to have broken into Beth Israel through a window and doused the synagogue’s library with gasoline before setting it ablaze. The fire and the subsequent damage destroyed much of the interior of the building, which also housed the Institute of Southern Jewish Life. Pittman faces state and federal charges. A federal judge ruled in August that he would undergo a psychiatric evaluation, though a county clerk said that has not yet taken place, and an updated trial date has not yet been set. Two of Beth Israel’s Torahs were completely destroyed by the fire; some of the others were damaged beyond repair. A Holocaust Torah survived the blaze . The congregation adapted immediately: for the adult bat mitzvah of Tamar Sharp, held a week after the arson, Beth Israel borrowed a Torah from Hattiesburg and prayer books from Memphis. Beth Israel Congregation has been meeting at Northminster Baptist Church since an arson attack in Jan. 2026. Photo by Elijah Hurewitz-Ravitch ‘We ain’t going nowhere’ The building itself largely survived the fire. Built to evoke Abraham’s tent with its pale color and low-slung roof, Beth Israel has been compared to a fortress, with concrete buttresses and a steel framework. (One congregant said that if there was ever a tornado coming for Jackson, she’d head straight to Beth Israel.) Much of the damage to the interior is the result of steam that roared through the building, trapped, when firemen hosed down the exterior. In the weeks after the fire, some congregants “advocated for just knocking it down and starting over,” said Sheila Hailey, Beth Israel’s executive director. “There was some talk about, ‘Well, now’s the time to move out of Jackson.’” Many Beth Israel members have already moved to Ridgeland and Madison, wealthy suburbs to the north. But the idea of relocating didn’t go far. “It’s just flight,” Hailey said. “Jackson is where Beth Israel has always been.” A prayer book burnt in a Jan. 2026 arson attack at Beth Israel Congregation in Jackson, Mississippi, is now on display at the Museum of the Southern Jewish Experience in New Orleans. Photo by Elijah Hurewitz-Ravitch The arson — seemingly intended to halt worship at Beth Israel — appears to have had the opposite effect. What Pittman did, said Mark Seros, a new member, “shored things up — ‘We ain’t going nowhere, buddy.’” Though Beth Israel’s building remains unusable, its congregants agree that their community has emerged from the attack strengthened, with renewed vigor to keep Judaism alive in Mississippi. “We’re smaller as a community, number-wise,” said Ben Russell, a convert to Judaism who became the Jackson, Mississippi synagogue’s student rabbi just six months before the fire. “However, I think today we are a little more tight knit, a little more proud to be present, proud to be Jewish.” Deep roots Jews have lived in Mississippi since before it was a state. A handful first arrived at the end of the 18th century, and communities eventually sprung up in towns along the Mississippi River. At the peak of its Jewish population, the state was home to nearly two dozen congregations, according to a 1940 WPA survey. For decades, the center of Mississippi Jewry was the Delta — a marshy, agricultural region and the birthplace of the Blues. In the years after World War II, as the children of peddlers and store owners became doctors and lawyers, Jackson, the capital, emerged as the state’s largest community. Other Jewish communities in the state dried up; even a city like Woodville, once dubbed “Little Jerusalem,” had lost nearly all of its Jews by 1910. Beth Israel is now one of only two congregations in Mississippi that have a full-time rabbi. Related The Holocaust Torah that survived a Mississippi synagogue fire was brought there by the state’s only survivor Founded in 1861, it has always been Jackson’s lone synagogue — “the only game in town,” as Robert Emmich, a longtime member with deep roots in the state, put it. Jackson’s Jewish community has never been able to support two congregations, according to Stuart Rockoff, director of the Mississippi Humanities Council and an expert on Southern Jewish history. Beth Israel, then, has “always been a congregation that had to accommodate people from different backgrounds,” he said. Beth Israel dedicated its midcentury modern building in a leafy neighborhood in northeast Jackson in 1967. Six months later, seeking to retaliate against then-Rabbi Perry Nussbaum’s outspoken support for the Civil Rights movement, the Ku Klux Klan bombed the synagogue . Within a few weeks, prayer services resumed. Mississippi Jews these days number around 1,500, with roughly 650 in greater Jackson. Some two or three dozen show up for services on a typical Shabbat. “We’ve never been able to take our Judaism for granted — because we were the only ones,” said Zach Shemper, Beth Israel’s president. The great-grandson of a metal recycler, Shemper helps run a large scrap company near downtown Jackson. In Jackson, “it’s not like you can shul shop,” said Michele Schipper, who grew up in Beth Israel and once served as president. “There’s one place.” Disagreements abound — “there are people in this congregation that cannot talk to each other on politics,” said Hailey — but names like “Trump” are usually checked at the door. A ‘second soul’ Despite the tragedy earlier this year, Beth Israel is “not quitting, not giving up, not closing shop,” Hailey said. The arson and its aftermath have brought out what she called a “combativeness” in many congregants, adding: “We’re here, and we’re going to stay here, and we’re going to rebuild.” Just days after the arson, Shemper asked Peter Sharp, a local hotel developer, to chair a rebuilding committee. The eight-person team first met at the end of January and then worked to solicit suggestions from congregants. Meanwhile, Shemper recruited a camp friend with a remediation company; the business partner of a former Beth Israel member volunteered the services of his construction firm. Chris Myers, another member, is a principal at the architectural firm designing the building’s new interior. Related How an ‘all-American boy’ became a Mississippi synagogue arson suspect The day of the fire, Tad Orkin, a lifelong Beth Israel member, ducked into the building and hauled out the synagogue’s blueprints. “Those plans are like gold,” Orkin said. As a teen in the 1960s, he watched the building be constructed almost every day after school. Now, he is eager to see what the new design will look like. Not everything is gone: the Jerusalem stone ark survived and is still in the building; the pews are sitting in a storage container outdoors. But half of the benches in the new sanctuary will have armrests, befitting an aging congregation. “We’re not making a bigger sanctuary, because it’s not like we’re gonna have 50 more Jews, or 100 more Jews,” Shemper said, “unless everybody just starts procreating.” An architectural rendering of the updated sanctuary at Beth Israel Congregation in Jackson, Mississippi. Photo by Elijah Hurewitz-Ravitch Other updates reflect the changes to Beth Israel’s demographic makeup: several classrooms will be repurposed and restrooms made more accessible; new TV screens will provide community updates. The synagogue is also getting, for the first time, a dedicated security booth — and, potentially, a full-time security detail. A new memorial outside will commemorate both the 1967 bombing and the 2026 arson — acts committed in different contexts but that have each kindled a spirit of resilience. The fire was set in the library in the eastern end of the synagogue; that space was the most heavily damaged. For years, it was where a committed group of Beth Israel members would gather for Saturday morning services, which lean Conservative. Soon, the room will become a dedicated chapel, and the library will move to the north side of the building. Beth Israel’s construction budget came in much higher than temple leadership expected, Sharp said. The roughly 8,000 unsolicited donations that Beth Israel has received since the arson and the money from the insurance payout won’t cover the entire cost, so the synagogue has formed a new development committee to work on bridging the gap. Workers are set to begin prepping the building this week for reconstruction, Sharp said. He expects the building will be ready by spring 2028. For Russell, Beth Israel has a renewed sense of purpose and of self. “We talk in Judaism about receiving your second neshama — your second soul — on Shabbat,” he said, “and on some level, this has been a re-souling for us. As we build and continue to move forward, it’s going to be in a space that doesn’t take our Judaism for granted. Tragedy has a way of reorienting you in a way that nothing else can.” Related Opinion: An arsonist torched a Mississippi synagogue. It feels hauntingly familiar. The post Mississippi Jews begin rebuilding synagogue after arson attack. ‘We ain’t going nowhere’ appeared first on The Forward .

items.title: Study reveals nine deaths, seven of them British patients, from common painkiller used in Spain
items.author: Oriol Güell Domínguez
items.preview: Research suggests UK citizens have up to 120 times higher risk than Spaniards of suffering serious reactions to a drug called metamizole, whose most popular brand name is Nolotil and which is banned in the US
items.content: A presentation at the recent congress of the Spanish Society of Hospital Pharmacy (SEFH) reveals previously unknown data highlighting safety concerns, especially among UK citizens, about a common drug called metamizole (also known as dipyrone and sometimes called “Mexican aspirin” in the United States, where it is banned). That molecule is the active ingredient in Nolotil — Spain’s best-selling branded drug, regularly prescribed for pain and high fever. Seguir leyendo

items.title: سهمیه سوخت رانندگان اسنپ و تپسی متناسب با پیمایش اصلاح می‌شود
items.author: آی‌تی‌ایران
items.preview: اصلاح نحوه تخصیص سهمیه سوخت متناسب با پیمایش، اطلاع‌رسانی میزان سهمیه به کاربران راننده تاکسی‌های اینترنتی و رفع موانع دوگانه‌سوز کردن خودروها، سه محور نشست مشترک نمایندگان اسنپ و تپسی با مدیرعامل و معاونان شرکت ملی پالایش و پخش فرآورده‌های نفتی ایران بود. این نشست در پی اعلام آم
items.content: اصلاح نحوه تخصیص سهمیه سوخت متناسب با پیمایش، اطلاع‌رسانی میزان سهمیه به کاربران راننده تاکسی‌های اینترنتی و رفع موانع دوگانه‌سوز کردن خودروها، سه محور نشست مشترک نمایندگان اسنپ و تپسی با مدیرعامل و معاونان شرکت ملی پالایش و پخش فرآورده‌های نفتی ایران بود . این نشست در پی اعلام آمادگی شرکت ملی پالایش برای دریافت بازخوردها و شنیدن مشکلات کاربران راننده تاکسی‌های اینترنتی، با هدف بررسی راهکارهای بهبود اجرای طرح تخصیص سهمیه سوخت، برگزار شد . در این نشست، دغدغه کاربران راننده درباره تناسب سهمیه سوخت با میزان فعالیت آن‌ها مورد بررسی قرار گرفت و مقرر شد نحوه تخصیص سهمیه بر اساس پیمایش اصلاح شود . هدف از این بازنگری، پاسخ‌گویی بهتر به نیاز سوخت کاربران راننده‌ای است که برای کسب درآمد در تاکسی‌های اینترنتی فعالیت می‌کنند . بی‌اطلاعی از دریافت سهمیه و میزان آن، از دیگر نگرانی‌های مطرح‌شده بود؛ موضوعی که برنامه‌ریزی کاربران راننده برای ادامه فعالیت را با ابهام روبه‌رو می‌کند . برای رفع این مشکل، مقرر شد پس از تخصیص سهمیه، میزان آن از طریق مسیرهای اطلاع‌رسانی، از جمله پیامک یا اعلان در اپلیکیشن، به ناوگان تاکسی‌های اینترنتی اعلام شود . همچنین، با توجه به توقف طرح دوگانه‌سوز کردن خودروها، ضرورت فراهم شدن امکان استفاده مجدد کاربران راننده متقاضی از تسهیلات این طرح مطرح شد . در این زمینه، موانع مربوط به تامین مالی و تجهیزات بررسی شد و شرکت ملی پالایش و پخش فرآورده‌های نفتی برای پیگیری رفع این موانع و فراهم کردن زمینه از سرگیری طرح قول مساعد داد . تاکسی‌های اینترنتی پیگیری این مطالبات را تا اجرایی شدن اصلاحات و روشن شدن نحوه بهره‌مندی کاربران راننده از سهمیه سوخت و تسهیلات دوگانه‌سوز کردن خودروها ادامه خواهند داد . The post سهمیه سوخت رانندگان اسنپ و تپسی متناسب با پیمایش اصلاح می‌شود appeared first on ITIRAN | آی تی ایران .

items.content: Ұлттық валюта – теңге күніне орай Қазақстан Республикасының Президенті жанындағы Қазақстанның стратегиялық зерттеулер институтының бас бухгалтері Әділбек Камзенов ҚР Қаржы министрлігінің «Қаржы саласының үздігі» төсбелгісімен марапатталды. Бұл марапат оның ел қаржы жүйесін дамытуға қосқан үлесі мен адал, білікті еңбегінің лайықты бағасы болды. Әділбек Камзенов Институтта бухгалтерлік есеп пен қаржылық есептілікті ұйымдастырады, бюджетті жоспарлау және мемлекеттік сатып алу жұмыстарына атсалысады. Сообщение ҚСЗИ маманы Қаржы министрлігінің ведомстволық марапатына ие болды появились сначала на ҚАЗАҚСТАН РЕСПУБЛИКАСЫНЫҢ ПРЕЗИДЕНТІ ЖАНЫНДАҒЫ ҚАЗАҚСТАННЫҢ СТРАТЕГИЯЛЫҚ ЗЕРТТЕУЛЕР ИНСТИТУТЫ .

items.title: New Working Group Seeks Justice for Critical Mineral Mining Communities
items.author: Isaiah Esipisu
items.preview: A coalition of African civil society organisations, representatives from the Africa Institute of Resilience Studies (an independent organisation working in research, policy, training and capacity development), and representatives from the Bank–Civil Society Coalition, which bring
items.content: ACSEA's Dr Augustine Njamnshi. Credit ACSEA By Isaiah Esipisu ANTALYA, Türkiye, Nov 16 2026 (IPS) A coalition of African civil society organisations, representatives from the Africa Institute of Resilience Studies (an independent organisation working in research, policy, training and capacity development), and representatives from the Bank–Civil Society Coalition, which brings together seven major regional networks and civil society organisations working on climate and energy, have launched the African Non-State Actors Working Group on Critical Minerals on the sidelines of COP 31 in Antalya, Türkiye. The launch comes amid growing concerns over environmental degradation and social suffering among communities living in energy-transition mineral-rich areas in Africa, where people bear the burden of forced displacement, loss of livelihoods and human rights abuses, with very limited or sometimes no benefits at all. “Our shared purpose is to advance accountable, people-centred and nature-positive critical mineral development in Africa, with decent work at its core,” said Dr Augustine Njamnshi, the Executive Director at the African Coalition for Sustainable Energy and Access (ACSEA). “Africa’s mineral wealth must create lasting value within Africa through local processing, refining, manufacturing and regional value chains that strengthen productive capabilities, support African ownership and improve community wellbeing,” he told delegates attending the UN climate summit in Antalya (COP31). From cobalt, copper, coltan, lithium and other strategic minerals in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and parts of Zambia, to lithium projects in Zimbabwe and graphite in Mozambique, communities in mining areas continue to face poverty, environmental damage, unsafe working conditions, displacement, conflict and limited participation in decisions affecting their land and livelihoods. “I believe the new working group will bring additional energy if it places affected communities, Indigenous Peoples, artisanal miners and African civil-society organisations at the centre,” said Appolinaire Zagabe, the Executive Director at the DRC Climate Change Network ( Réseau sur le Changement Climatique RDC – RCCRDC ). The working group committed to building an all representative and action-orientated platform for collective engagement, bringing together organised labour, frontline communities, women and youth organisations, researchers, environmental movements and other African non-state actors. “We will organise our work around four connected functions based on ideas and evidence, policy and advocacy, accountability, and voice and participation,” said Njamnshi. “Our goal is to advance freedom of association and collective bargaining, living wages, safe workplaces, social protection, skills development and the inclusion of artisanal and small-scale miners,” he told the delegates in Antalya. According to Philip Kilonzo, the Head of Policy, Advocacy and Communication at the Pan African Climate Justice Alliance (PACJA), the working group will help bridge existing gaps in evidence and coordinated advocacy on critical minerals and a just energy transition. “It will strengthen our collective efforts to promote accountable governance of Africa’s critical mineral resources, ensuring that their exploitation contributes meaningfully to the development and well-being of African people,” he told IPS. To kick off, the working group will begin by developing shared evidence and priorities through an African Critical Minerals Issues Paper, wider consultations and a common African Non-State-Actor’s position. “We will explore a Labour and Just Transition Brief and an accountability framework or scorecard examining decision-making, ownership, working conditions, the distribution of benefits and responsibility for risks,” said Njamnshi. “These products will be developed through consultation and are not presented as completed instruments at this launch.” Interested organisations and constituencies, including African civil society organisations, trade unions, mining-affected communities, Indigenous Peoples and local communities, women’s and youth organisations, researchers and other non-state actors have also been invited to contribute their knowledge, experience and proposals through the ACSEA secretariat. At the same time, RCCRDC, as a national civil-society platform in DRC and an accredited observer to the UNFCCC and UNEP, has raised community concerns in climate and energy-transition discussions at COP 31. “We advocate for early community participation, transparent mineral governance, environmental protection, decent employment, local value addition and enforceable benefit-sharing,” said Zagabe. “We have also proposed a legally binding one percent contribution on final products linked to critical and energy transition minerals to go to community development,” he told IPS. So far, the DRC Mining Code provides for community development agreements and an annual allocation of 0.3% of mining companies’ turnover for community development. However, according to Zagabe, implementation, transparency and community oversight have always been inconsistent. “Our central message is clear, that the global energy transition must not reproduce exploitation, conflict and inequality in mineral-producing countries,” he said. “Communities must have decision-making power, legal protection and a fair share of the wealth generated from their resources.” As the world transitions to clean energy while reducing dependence on fossils, demand for critical energy transition minerals is growing every day, and Africa holds a significant share of them. However, the continent constantly exports raw materials and semi-finished products to the developed world, while receiving very little share of the massive wealth created from the sector. According to a UN report , countries and mining communities are often left with degraded landscapes, limited services, a few lasting economic opportunities and very little to show from the harnessing of their mineral resource wealth. And now, at COP 31, African leaders and civil society representatives say that it is time for Africa to take charge. “As Africa, the way to go is to ensure that we don’t just release our critical resources to the developed world, who eventually leave us with problems,” said Dr Benjamin Mandewere, the Principal Climate Change Adaptation Officer in the Ministry of Environment, Climate and Wildlife in Zimbabwe. “We also have to ensure that environmental and social impact assessments not only look at particular places but also take local communities on board to ensure that their voices are heard and they also benefit from these resources,” he told the delegates in Antalya. items.content: متابعة/المدى استضافت لجنة الأمر النيابي (198) الخاصة بالتحقيق في ملف تهريب النفط، اليوم الاثنين، قيادات أمنية رفيعة في وزارتي الدفاع والداخلية لاستعراض نتائج التحقيقات ومواقع التهريب في منطقتي جرف النصر وكركوك، فيما تقرر تأجيل الاجتماع المقرر مع وزيري الدفاع والداخلية ومدير مكتب القائد العام للقوات المسلحة إلى الساعة السابعة مساءً. وأفاد عضو اللجنة، بدر الفحل، في تصريح للوكالة الرسمية، تابعته (المدى)، بأن "اللجنة عقدت اجتماعاً مع القيادات الأمنية في وزارتي الدفاع والداخلية، ضم وكيل الاستخبارات وقائد عمليات كركوك وعدداً من القادة الأمنيين، للوقوف على مستجدات التحقيق في ملف تهريب النفط في جرف النصر وكركوك". وبيّن الفحل أن "اللجنة استعرضت خلال الاجتماع مجمل التحقيقات والمواقع التي شهدت عمليات التهريب في المنطقتين"، لافتاً إلى "تأجيل الاستضافة الخاصة بوزيري الدفاع والداخلية ومدير مكتب القائد العام للقوات المسلحة إلى الساعة السابعة من مساء اليوم". The post لجنة تهريب النفط تستضيف قيادات أمنية لبحث ملفات كركوك والجرف appeared first on جريدة المدى .

art_full:1a6tw6r.title: Guinea: Shutdwon of illegal gold mining, arrests and deportations spark regional outcry
art_full:1a6tw6r.content:
In Siguiri, northeastern Guinea, the gold rush has come to an abrupt end. "To date, 1,263 people, including Guineans, Burkinabe, Malians, Togolese, Nigerians, Ivorians, and Ghanaians, have been arrested and taken to Conakry for legal proceedings," Guinea's army spokesman, General Mamadou Aliou Sow, said. He added that officers from the Criminal Investigation Division, the National Police, and the National Gendarmerie are currently conducting interrogations.

The operation follows the ban on illegal gold mining in the Siguiri administrative region. According to Guinean authorities, the aim is to stop mining practices considered harmful to the environment. Uncontrolled gold mining depletes the soil, destroy vegetation and choke waterways.

"We know that there have recently been various forms of gold mining here involving the use of chemicals that can destroy the environmentand pollute our water sources," Toumany Sangare, chairman of the Siguiri civil society council, told DW.

The closure of the mining sites is having a significant impact on the local economy. For many workers, it means the sudden loss of their main source of income. DW spoke with young gold panners from Burkina Faso who had been driven out of Siguiri. Some said they had walked more than 200 km (124 miles) to the Malian capital, Bamako.

"We tried our luck, but just as we were beginning to feel hopeful, we were told to leave," Noufa, in his early 20s, who arrived in Siguiri in early October to work in a small mine, told DW. Another Burkinabe, who goes by the name Mc One, told DW he set out for Siguiri to earn money to provide for his elderly parents and relatives. "I left just under five months ago. We went through very difficult times there."

Did Guinean authorities target foreigners?

Guinean authorities refute the allegation that the ban on gold mining specifically targeted foreigners, saying the measure applies to all illegal gold miners. The closure of the mine primarily affects Guineans, Mohamed Nabe, chairman of the Committee on Mining and Industry, told DW.

"Millions of Guineans are affected by this, compared to just a few thousand foreigners," Nabe said, adding that like everywhere else, there are cross-border population movements. "Of course, this can raise certain security concerns, but it was not the security aspect that motivated this decision. The main reasons are environmental in nature, as well as the need to better organize, structure, and regulate the mining sector."

The hidden cost of illegal gold mining in Ghana

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Supporting the move, Morissanda Kouyate, Guinea's Foreign Minister, said his country is not the only one to ban illegal gold mining. However, according to Burkina Faso's Minister of Security, Mahamadou Sana, the deported nationals were allegedly subjected to "cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment." He spoke of "brutality" and alleged that the operation had resulted in deaths and injuries.

Malian journalist Amadou Oumar Diallo also criticized the alleged brutality of the Guinean authorities. In his view, they violated human rights. "Normally, when you prevent someone from exercising their freedom, you also have to provide for them," Diallo told DW. "This care is expensive. Detention alone costs a lot of money. The Guinean government took the easy way out by refusing to adhere to these principles and deporting all these people."

While Burkina Faso strongly condemned the treatment of gold panners, Mali's leadership initially adopted a somewhat more restrained tone. Officially, Bamako described Guinea's decision to expel the miners as "sovereign."

Most recently, however, Mali's Prime Minister, Major General Abdoulaye Maiga, spoke of a "humanitarian catastrophe." On November 8, he traveled to Kouremale on the border between Mali and Guinea, where dozens of deported Malians were returning to the country. Given the close ties between Mali and Guinea, Maiga regretted the lack of coordination between the two countries.

Currently, authorities in Mali and Burkina Faso are organizing efforts to assist their citizens: buses and trucks have been mobilized from both Bamako and Ouagadougou to bring the deported gold miners back to their home countries.

Parallel to the events in Siguiri, the Nimba Gold Refinery (NGR) has begun operations in Conakry. With this, Guinea joins other West African nations such as Burkina Faso, Mali, and Cote d'Ivoire. The Guinean government's goal is to refine 30% of the 70 metric tons (70,000 kg) of gold mined in the country domestically.

Dr. Ibrahim Diallo, a mining expert, suggested that the Guinean authorities may have wanted to bring the gold mines in Siguiri under their control to supply the Nimba Gold Refinery (NGR). "What's happening in Siguiri isn't gold panning. A gold panner doesn't use a bulldozer or an excavator."

Joining forces to protect Guinea's Tristao Islands

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick Schein, chairman of the Alliance for Responsible Mining (ARM), told DW that it made more sense for Guinea to build up reserves with domestic gold rather than imported gold. However, he also stressed that the gold must be certified to be internationally recognized.

He does not anticipate significant local demand, so exports are crucial. It remains to be seen whether the refinery in Conakry can be competitive in this regard. For jewelry manufacturing, for example, international-level technical expertise is required.

Another issue, according to the ARM chairman, is that the location of refining determines the gold's origin. "So if I'm in Guinea and import or buy gold that comes from another country, that gold becomes Guinean gold through local refining," Schein said. "If Guinea serves as a transit hub for gold from the subregion, it would—unintentionally—become a center for money laundering," he added.

According to Schein, tracing refined gold is harder than tracing raw gold. However, if the goal of refining [gold] in Guinea is to ensure better traceability, pay miners better wages and create a mercury-free processing chain, then that is a good initiative. "But now this must also be put into practice."

Mohamed Toure in Conakry and Mahamadou Kane in Bamako contributed to this article

This article was originally written in German
